blocks.h: A Note from the Author

This book began with a costume and an uncomfortable question that the costume makes it impossible to avoid: does moral authority come from the clothes and the institution, or from what a person actually does?
The honest answer, as far as I have been able to get to one, is neither, exactly — and the not-quite-answer is the reason this is a novel and not an essay.

I have wanted for a long time to write something that laughs. Everything in this imprint until now has been made in the dark, on purpose, and I do not regret any of it. But there is a particular register available in Persian that I have never used here and that I have been carrying around since childhood: a way of being funny about catastrophe that is not denial and is not bravery either, that runs underneath the whole culture like a service tunnel, and that is at its sharpest precisely where things are worst. A people who have had that much history done to them develop a sense of humour with load-bearing walls. Nader Fani talks the way my uncles talk. So does his daughter, which is the thing he cannot mention.
The other thing I wanted was to be fair to the coat.

It would have been very easy — and would have made a much stupider book — to write the clergy as villains and the fraud as the only honest man in the building. That is a satire I have no interest in. What interested me was the middle of it: the mid-fifties man with a bad back and a daughter's wedding to fund, who stopped believing twenty years ago and stays because eleven hundred people need somebody to bury their mothers properly, and who knows exactly what else his staying maintains. The garment that lets a man walk into the worst hour of a stranger's life is the same garment the careerists are wearing. It is the mercy and it is the crime and it is one object. That is not hypocrisy. That is the actual arrangement, in every institution I have ever looked at closely, and most of us are inside one.

A word on the smoke, since readers will assume I invented it. Esfand — wild rue — is burned in every taxi, shop and doorway in Iran to turn away the evil eye. It is sold in paper cones by children at traffic lights. It is also Peganum harmala, and it carries harmine and harmaline, the same compounds that form the backbone of ayahuasca; a number of scholars have argued that it was the original haoma of the Zoroastrian sacrifice. Nobody in Iran calls it a drug. It is what your grandmother does when you get a promotion. Burn enough of it in a stone room with no vent, over people who have been fasting and grieving and awake for three nights, and things happen. Everything in this book that occurs in that chamber is chemically and architecturally plausible, and none of it required anyone to be deceived about what they were breathing. The best hiding place is the category nobody looks at.

There is a film underneath all of this, and I would rather name it than have it noticed: Marmoulak, Kamal Tabrizi, 2004. I owe it the premise and the nerve. It was pulled from Iranian cinemas within weeks of becoming a hit. What it understood, and what I have tried to carry over, is that the sharp version of this story is not religion is a fraud. The sharp version is that religion without humanity is hollow, and a man with no credentials whatsoever may walk into genuine spirituality sideways, by accident, through compassion, while being extremely funny about it.
Nader would want me to add that he never carried a weapon.
Chew Z

PART ONE — THE WALL
Lessons One to Nine
LESSON 1
Knock first.
The stone in my gallbladder was the size of a chickpea, and it saved my life, which should tell you how God conducts His business. He does not send angels. He sends sediment.

I had been in Vakilabad [va-keel-aa-BAAD] four years by then and had made a study of the place the way a man makes a study of his own hand. There were eleven ways out of that building and I had ruled out ten of them by my second winter. The eleventh was medical, and the eleventh required an organ to betray me, and I had been waiting on that betrayal with the patience of a man waiting for a bus in a country where the buses have been discontinued.
I want to say something about patience, because it is the only virtue I have ever possessed and I would like it noted before we go any further.

I was a thief. I was not a good man and I was not a clever man, but I was a patient one, and in my trade patience is worth more than either. Anyone can go through a window. The art is in the four hours before the window, sitting in a stairwell with your hands folded, listening to a building settle, letting a family finish an argument two floors up and go to bed unhappy. I could sit in a stairwell longer than most men can sit in their own living rooms. I was famous for it, in the small and idiotic way that men in my line become famous for things.
I also never carried a weapon. Not once, not a knife, not a length of pipe, in twenty-seven years. I would like that noted here at the front where it can be found.
They called me Panjshanbeh [panj-shan-BEH]. Thursday.

I worked Thursday nights and only Thursday nights. There were reasons. Thursday night in Iran is the night the whole country goes to somebody's mother's house, and a family at somebody's mother's house is a family not at home, and a family not at home is a proposition. That was the practical reason and it was a good one. The other reason was that Friday is the holy day, and I did not want to be caught working on it, because I did not believe in God and saw no need to be rude to Him.
I have thought about that sentence a great deal since. At the time I considered it a joke.

The name was given to me by a man in Block Three who intended it as an insult and who was, in fairness, entitled to. Here he comes, he'd say, here comes the weekend. He died of something in his chest the winter before my transfer and I was sorrier than I expected to be, which is the whole of my eulogy for him and more than he got from anyone else.

I also wore reading glasses on jobs. I did not need them. I had discovered at nineteen that a man in reading glasses looks like a man with an appointment, and a man with an appointment is invisible in this country, because nobody has ever once had an appointment. Twenty-seven years I wore those glasses. I have never had my eyes tested. My eyes are excellent. That is not a boast, it is a complaint — a man with my eyes should have seen more coming.

And I knocked. Always. Before every door I ever opened that was not mine, I knocked, twice, unhurried, the way my father knocked on the doors of customers who owed him money. If someone answered I became a man looking for an address, and I apologised, and I apologised beautifully, and I left. I have knocked on six hundred doors in this country and apologised at perhaps eighty of them, and I want you to hold onto that number, because later on somebody is going to tell you that I am a man who takes what he wants, and I want you to have the arithmetic in front of you when they do.
Now. The infirmary.

They put me on a bed by the window because I was not violent and because the orderly's cousin knew a man I had once not informed on. I lay there for two days with my knees up and something in my side turning over like a slow engine, and on the second afternoon Sarhang Zaker [sar-HANG ZAA-ker] came to see me.

You should understand about Zaker. In the films the warden is fat and corrupt and sells the prisoners' rice. Zaker was thin, and honest, and had never taken a rial in his life, and this is why he was the most frightening man I have ever met. He had a theory. Corrupt men do not have theories. Corrupt men have appetites, and an appetite can be fed, but a theory has to be proved, and he intended to prove his on me.
His theory was that men are made good by pressure.

He said it kindly. He always said it kindly. He sat down on the plastic chair beside my bed, and he asked after my pain, and he meant it, and then he said that he had my file and that in his experience a man of forty-six with a body beginning to fail him is a man at the exact temperature where change becomes possible. He said the word change the way a doctor says the name of a procedure he has performed many times successfully.

He had statistics. I want to be honest about this, because it costs me something. He had statistics and they were good. Fewer of his men came back than came back from anywhere else in the province, and he knew the number, and he did not exaggerate it, and he did not need to.
"You have a daughter," he said.
"I have a photograph," I said.

He let that sit. He was very good at letting things sit. Then he stood, and he put the plastic chair back exactly where he had found it — exactly, he adjusted it, I watched him do it — and he said that he would see me when I came back from the hospital, and that we would talk again, and that he was not in a hurry.
That was the sentence that decided it. Not the daughter. I am not in a hurry.

Because I knew, lying there with my chickpea, that he was telling the truth. He was not in a hurry. He had eight years of me and a theory to prove and all the time in the world, and he would apply pressure to me kindly, at room temperature, for eight years, and at the end of it I would come out the other side improved, and I would be sixty, and I would be good, and I would be finished.
So I would like to be clear about what I wanted, that afternoon, before any of the rest of it happened. I did not want to be free. Freedom is for young men and people with plans.
I wanted to not be improved.
LESSON 2
A locked door is only an opinion.

They took me to Mashhad [mash-HAD] in a Peugeot with a broken window winder and a driver who spent the entire ninety minutes explaining that his brother-in-law had been cheated on a shipment of pistachios. I was chained to the seat frame. I said no and of course and what a world in the appropriate places. I have always been a good passenger.

Here is a thing about hospitals that I knew and Zaker did not, because Zaker had never stolen anything: a hospital is not a building. A hospital is nine or ten buildings that hate each other, joined by corridors, administered by people who are on strike from a department they cannot name. There is no such thing as security in a hospital. There is only paperwork, and paperwork can be outwaited.

They put me in a pre-operative bay on the third floor with a curtain on a rail, and they took the chain off my wrist because the anaesthetist required it, and the guard went to find a form, and I lay there and did what I have always done, which is nothing at all, for a long time, with my hands folded.

Two hours. I want that on the record too. Two hours I lay in that bay with my wrist free and I did not move, because it was three in the afternoon and the corridors were full, and a man who runs at three in the afternoon is a man in a story that ends badly.
At ten past five they wheeled someone into the next bay and drew the curtain and went away and did not come back.
I could see his feet.

I want to describe this correctly, because it is the hinge of my entire life and I have heard it described wrongly by people who were not there. There was no moment of decision. There was no whisper. Nobody in that room was struck by lightning. I saw a pair of feet in a pair of good shoes, and above the shoes a chair, and on the chair a folded pile of clothes, and I thought — and this is the whole of my thinking, in its entirety, I have examined it many times since and found nothing else in it — nobody is watching that chair.
That is not a religious experience. That is a trade.

I got up. My side complained. I went through the curtain like a man going to ask about a bedpan, and there he was, and he was dead. I do not know what he died of. I have wondered. I have wondered a great deal more than you would expect. He was perhaps sixty-five and he had a good face, a really quite good face, the kind of face you get from a life of being listened to, and his hands were arranged on his chest by somebody who had cared enough to arrange them.
I said, out loud, in the empty bay, "Excuse me."
Then I took his clothes.

The qaba [gha-BAA], the long coat, and the abaya [a-baa-YAA], the black cloak that goes over it, and the wound cloth of the turban, which is called an amameh [ah-maa-MEH], and which I did not know was called an amameh, and which I did not look at, because I was folding it into my armpit under my hospital gown and counting the seconds on the corridor outside.
I want to be very clear. I did not look at the colour.

I have been accused of many things and I have earned most of them, but not that. I did not stand in that bay and calculate. I did not think black, ah, black, that is the good one. I did not know there was a good one. I had lived forty-six years in the Islamic Republic of Iran and could not have told you, at gunpoint, that a black turban meant one thing and a white turban meant another. Nobody could. Ask them. Ask the next ten people you meet. They will all say of course I know that and then they will change the subject.

His identity card was in the coat pocket. I did not look at that either, not then. I took the shoes as well. They were half a size too big and I wore them for the next eleven months and they ruined my feet, and I want it understood that everything that came afterwards — the town, the women, the smoke, the girl, all of it — was conducted by a man in the wrong shoes.

I dressed in the stairwell between the third and fourth floors, which took four minutes, three of them spent on the turban, which I wound the way a man winds a turban who has only ever seen one at a distance, on television, on somebody who was shouting.
It looked, I later learned, appalling.
Nobody said anything for six weeks.
LESSON 3
Never run from a place you can walk out of.
The corridor. The lifts. The lobby with the fish tank that had no fish in it.

I did not hurry. Hurrying is what they watch for. I put my hands behind my back the way old men do and I went down the stairs at the pace of a man with a bad hip, which required no acting, and I came out into the ground floor concourse at twenty to six in the evening with my heart going like a bird in a bag.
And a boy held the door for me.

Then a woman moved out of my way. Then an orderly pushing a trolley of linen stopped the trolley — stopped it entirely, in the middle of the corridor, and stood back, and waited, and gave me a small bow of the head — so that I could pass.

I did not understand what was happening. I want you to sit with that, because I have had twenty years of people assuming I walked out of that hospital in a glow of criminal triumph, and the truth is that I walked out of it in a state of low-grade panic, convinced that every one of these people had recognised me and was being strange about it.
A man at the pharmacy window turned around, saw me, and lowered his eyes.
I got as far as the car park before I understood, and what I understood was still wrong, but it was closer. I thought: they are afraid of the clothes.

That was the third lesson and it took me four more months to correct it. They were not afraid. Fear I would have recognised — I have made a career out of being in rooms with frightened people. This was something else and it was much worse and I did not have a word for it yet.

The gate had a guard on it. There is always a guard. He had a clipboard and a moustache that had taken him a decade and he looked up as I approached and my whole body prepared itself, in the old way, for the sprint I was not going to be able to manage.
He said, "Salaam alaykom, Haj Aqa [haaj AA-ghaa]."
Haj Aqa. Sir. Reverend sir. The thing you call a cleric when you do not know his name.

And I heard myself say — in a voice I had never used before, a voice that came up out of me the way water comes up out of a cracked pipe, deeper than my own, slower than my own, a voice I had been carrying around inside me for forty-six years without ever once having a use for it —
"Alaykom as-salaam."
He waved me through and went back to his clipboard.
I got fifty metres up the road before I had to stop and put my hand on a wall.
LESSON 4
If a stranger kisses your hand, find out why before you enjoy it.

The bus station at Mashhad is a place where the entire nation stands in a queue and complains about the queue, and I have always found it restful. I bought a ticket to the first town I did not recognise on the board. I paid with money from the dead man's coat, seventy thousand tomans [toh-MAANS] and a receipt for a repaired watch, and I have thought about that watch on and off for twenty years, sitting uncollected in a shop in Mashhad, ticking.
The driver would not take my fare.

I held out the ticket and he waved it away with the back of his hand, twice, the second time with a small pained expression as though I had suggested something indecent, and then he took my hand — took it, in both of his — and he kissed it.
On the back. Near the knuckle. A dry, quick, entirely serious kiss.
Then he said, "Ziyarat qabul, Aqa Sayyid."
May your pilgrimage be accepted, master sayyid.
I sat down in the fourth row.

Now, I want to describe my interior state at this moment as precisely as I am able, because everyone who has ever heard this story assumes that I was delighted, and I was not delighted, I was in something close to physical distress. I had been given back my money. A stranger had kissed my hand. And I did not know the word he had used.

There was a man beside me, sixty, going to see his sister, who told me so within ninety seconds without my asking a single question. I let him talk for twenty minutes. Then I said, in the new voice, in the slow one, "And what do people say now, brother? Out in the world."
Which is a sentence that means nothing at all, and which I had already discovered got you eleven minutes of material.
Somewhere in the eleven minutes he said, "— and of course, they see the black and they think, ah, a sayyid [saa-YED], this one is from the House, this one is of the blood, God keep them —"
The black.
I did not move. I have sat in stairwells for four hours. I did not move.

I understood, in the space of about four seconds, sitting on a bus in the province of Khorasan [kho-raa-SAAN] with my hands folded in my lap, that the article of clothing on my head was not a uniform. A uniform is a claim about your job. This was a claim about my great-grandfather, and his, and his, running back thirteen centuries to a man in Arabia, and it was not a claim you could make by studying, or by being appointed, or by being good. It was a claim you could only make by being born, and it could not be granted and it could not be revoked and it could not be earned, and I had taken it off a chair.
I want to record that my first coherent thought was about my father.

My father, Bahman Fani [bah-MAN faa-NEE], locksmith, of Nasser Khosrow [NAA-ser khos-ROW], prayed five times a day for fifty-one years and cheated every customer who ever entered his shop, and when I asked him about this once — I was eleven, I remember the exact tile I was standing on — he looked at me with real bewilderment and said, God asked me to pray. He did not ask me to charge fairly. He kept a ledger with God in it, my father. Debits and credits. And by his own accounting he was always, somehow, very slightly ahead.
And I sat on that bus and I thought: the old thief is going to be extremely pleased about this.

My second thought was practical. I turned it over the way you turn over a lock. Take it off? Then I am a man in a stolen coat with a shaved neck and no papers and my face on a list in Vakilabad by tomorrow morning. Explain? To whom?
Give it back?

And that, I am sorry to say, is where the whole thing was settled, on the fourth row of a bus, in a sentence I said inside my own head with a small shrug, and which I have never once been able to improve upon:
Well. I can't very well give it back now.
LESSON 5
Ask for a town nobody wants.

Shurabad [shoo-raa-BAAD] means Salt-Town, which is not a nickname. It sits at the edge of a flat white nothing that was a lake in the time of the Sasanians and has been a rumour ever since, and the salt gets into the walls, and the walls come apart slowly from the inside, and everyone there has the same low, patient cough.
Nine hundred people. One road in, which is also the road out, which is a thing I noted immediately and did not think about carefully enough.

I chose it off the board because it was the last stop and because I calculated — correctly — that a town at the end of a road has no traffic in it, and a place with no traffic has no watchers. I intended to be there twelve days. Twelve days to grow the beard out properly, to work out what to do about papers, and then east and over, where a man with a beard and no history can be a great many things.
I have never in my life made a plan that survived contact with a bus timetable.

We came in at ten past nine at night. The bus stops in Shurabad at the top of the square, by the mosque and the shrine, which is called Emamzadeh Nur [eh-maam-zaa-DEH NOOR], the Shrine of the Light, and which is a small blue dome over the grave of a person whose identity has been the subject of a polite and unresolved local argument for four hundred years.
There were nine men waiting in the square.
I saw them through the window as we came up the hill and I did my arithmetic, which was: nine men, night, no women, a bus. And I concluded: somebody on this bus is in trouble.
I let everyone else off first. This is a habit. You learn more from the back.

Then I came down the steps into the cold with the dead man's bag in my hand, and the whole nine of them came forward at once like water finding a drain, and an old man at the front of them took my hand in both of his and said —
"Sayyid Hadi. Thank God. Thank God. Eleven days we've been meeting that bus."
Eleven days.

I have been asked, many times, why I did not simply say no. Why I did not say, in that square, brother, there has been an error, I am not the man. And I have given many answers over the years, most of them flattering to me and all of them false, and here is the true one:
Because he was seventy-one years old and he was standing in a cold square at nine o'clock at night, for the eleventh night, and he was so happy.
That is it. That is the entire moral architecture of my decision. I have examined it under better light than this and there is nothing else in there.

His name was Haj Rasoul Sarmadi [haaj ra-SOOL sar-maa-DEE] and he was the trustee of the shrine, and he had a laugh like a door in a draught, and he was the coldest thing in that town, and it would be two months before I found out.
He said, "You must be destroyed. Was it the road? It's the road. It's always the road."
And I said, in the voice, in the slow one, "It was the road."

And nine men laughed, because it was the road, it is always the road, and one of them took my bag away from me by force, in the way of this country, where a bag is a thing you must be relieved of by a stranger before hospitality can be considered to have begun, and we all walked up the hill together in the dark towards the little blue dome, and I turned my head once, in the way that I have, and confirmed that the road behind us went nowhere at all.
LESSON 6
Accept the room. The room is the alibi.

The custodian's quarters were two rooms and a yard behind the shrine, with a stove that worked and a window that did not, and a carpet that had been beaten so many times it had achieved a kind of transparency. Haj Rasoul walked me through it holding a paraffin lamp and apologising continuously, in the way of a man showing you a house he is very proud of.
"It's small," he said, of a room I would have paid rent for in Tehran.
"It's more than enough."
"It's a disgrace. The last one had the damp. Not this room. The other room. But it's the same wall, so." He shrugged at the wall. The wall did not respond. "You'll say if there's anything."
"I'll say."
"He won't say," he told the lamp. "They never say."

I unpacked a dead man's bag in front of a stranger, which is an activity I recommend to anyone who believes they have nerve. Three books. A pair of spectacles in a hard case. A comb. A tin of the little wire hooks you use to hang a lamp from a beam. A photograph of a woman, taken in a studio, in the seventies, who was either his mother or his wife and who I have never been able to decide about.

I put the books on the shelf spine-out and I did not open one of them for nine days, and when I finally did, on the ninth night, with the door locked, I discovered that I could read perhaps one word in four, and that the one word was usually and.
I have to tell you about the money, because it is the shabbiest part of this and I have never once got out of it cleanly.

There was a tin. Haj Rasoul showed it to me that first night with the lamp in his other hand, in the alcove by the stove, and he lifted the lid so I could see, and inside it was the shrine's small cash — the nazr [NAZR] money, the vow money, what people leave when they want something and what they leave when they got it. Perhaps four million tomans in notes with a rubber band around them.
He said, "For the kitchen, the oil, the whitewash, whatever comes."
And he left me alone with it and went home.
Now. I had come out of a hospital nine hours earlier with seventy thousand tomans and a receipt for a watch. That tin was a border.
That tin was papers, and a truck, and a man in Zahedan [zaa-heh-DAAN] who does not ask questions, and everything I had said I wanted since the moment I saw a pair of feet in good shoes.
I did not take it.

I want to be precise about why, because when I tell this story people want the answer to be that something moved in me, and nothing moved in me. I did not take it because the old man had shown it to me on the first night, which meant he wanted me to know it was there, which meant he was either the most trusting man in Khorasan or he was counting it, and I had been a professional for twenty-seven years and I did not survive twenty-seven years by taking the first tin I was shown.
He was counting it. Obviously he was counting it. It took me two months to be sure and eight weeks after that to understand what he had actually been measuring, which was not the money.
I slept badly and woke at five to the sound of a woman being extremely rude to a floor.

She was on her knees in the courtyard of the shrine with a bucket and a brush and a length of hose, working the flagstones by the door where nine hundred people a week come in off a salt flat, and she was addressing the ground in a low, fluent, entirely uninterrupted stream that I could not hear the words of and did not need to.
I stood in the dark of my doorway in a dead man's coat and watched a stranger insult a floor at five in the morning, and I thought: this is the first honest thing I have seen since Mashhad.
Then she looked up.

I have been looked at by police, by judges, by a man in Karaj [ka-RAJ] who had every reason to kill me and eventually decided not to. This was different in kind. She looked at me for about a second and a half, from her knees, with a wet brush in her hand, and something went across her face that was not deference and was not fear, and she said:
"You're up."
Not Haj Aqa. Not Sayyid. You're up.
"I'm up."
"There's tea." She went back to the floor. "It's terrible."
Her name was Shokouh Aramesh [sho-KOOH aa-raa-MESH], which means Splendour Calm, and which she found funnier than anyone else ever has.
The tea was terrible. I said so. It was the first true statement I had made in that town and it cost me about four years of what I had been.
LESSON 7
Say it, then stop talking.
I had four days before the first Friday and I spent them the way a condemned man spends his appeal.

I learned, from watching, from the back, from the doorway: when to stand, when to sit, which way to face, how long the pause is, what your hands do. Physical technique I can acquire. I have always been able to acquire physical technique. In four days I could stand and sit and turn like a man who had been doing it since he was six.
What I could not acquire in four days was the entire literary tradition of a civilisation.

On Friday there were two hundred and forty people in that mosque, which is more people than live in Shurabad, because they come in from the salt villages and from the road. Haj Rasoul had told everyone. Of course he had told everyone. The new sayyid is here. Eleven days they had met that bus and now the bus had produced.
I got up onto the two wooden steps of the minbar [MEM-bar] and I looked at two hundred and forty faces and my mind went out like a lamp.

Not blank. I want to be accurate. Blank would have been survivable. What I had instead was a very loud interior voice, my own, informing me at speed that I was about to be dragged out of a mosque by two hundred men and that it would take a while.
So I did the only thing I have ever done under pressure, which is nothing, for a long time.
Eleven seconds. I have since measured eleven seconds many times, in rooms, with a watch. It is an enormous amount of time. It is a geological era.
And in the eleventh second I watched the room change, and I did not understand what I was watching, and what I was watching was two hundred and forty people deciding that the silence was on purpose.
Then I opened my mouth, and something came out of it in Arabic.

I do not speak Arabic. I want this understood at the outset because everything that follows depends on it. I had eleven years of it at school in the way that every Iranian has eleven years of it at school, which is to say I could conjugate a verb in an exam in 1996 and can now recognise perhaps nine words in a newspaper. What I had instead was rhythm. I had forty-six years of standing in the back of rooms while men in this costume made this noise. I had the cadence of it in my body the way you have a pop song from your childhood in your body — every stress, every rise, every place where the voice drops and the room says salavat [sa-la-VAAT] — without one single word of the content.
So I made the noise.

I put a bismillah [bes-mel-LAAH] on the front of it — the In-the-name-of-God that opens everything — because everything has a bismillah on the front of it. I gave it the shape: the long vowel in the third position, the little climb, the pause, the drop. I made it four clauses long because four is the number of clauses. And I ended it low, and stopped.
Then I did not translate it.

That was the entire technique. That, right there, on the first Friday, by accident, out of terror — I did not translate it. I said the noise and then I closed my mouth and looked at the middle distance with an expression of mild sorrow.
And the room filled it in.

That is the thing I have spent twenty years trying to explain to people who were not in that mosque. They were not listening to the words. Nobody in that building was listening to the words; perhaps eleven of them could have followed the words. They were listening to the posture. And into eleven seconds of silence and four clauses of well-shaped nonsense, two hundred and forty people poured whatever they had brought in with them from the salt villages, and every one of them found in it exactly what he had come for, because he had put it there himself.
A man in the fourth row began to cry.

I want to tell you what that did to me and I find that I cannot, quite, even now. He was perhaps fifty. He had the cough. He was crying the way men cry in this country when they have permission, which is not quietly, and the men on either side of him put their hands on his back without looking at him, and after, in the courtyard, he came and took my hand and thanked me, thanked me, for what I had said about his brother.
I had said nothing about his brother. I did not know he had a brother. I still, to this day, do not know what happened to that man's brother.
I went back to the two rooms behind the shrine and I sat on the transparent carpet in the dark for about an hour.

And the thought I finally had — I would like to report that it was remorse. It was not remorse. It was a purely professional observation, and it arrived with the small cold click that a good lock makes, and it was this:
I have been doing this my entire life. I have simply been doing it at the wrong doors.
LESSON 8
The famous ones get checked. The obscure ones never do.
In my first week as a man of God I settled a wall, a goat, and a foreskin.

The wall was between two brothers and had been running for nine years. Both of them came to me on the Sunday, separately, each having been assured by the other's wife that I would see sense. I listened to the first one for fifty minutes and said nothing. Then I listened to the second one for fifty minutes and said nothing. Then I asked them both to come back on Tuesday, together, and on Tuesday I let them sit in my room in silence for a long time while I poured tea very slowly, and then I said:
"Which of you built it?"

Their father had built it. In 1974. Neither of them had built it and neither of them had thought about that for nine years, and one of them made a sound like a man stepping into cold water, and it was over, and they were both extremely grateful to me, and I had contributed exactly four words.

I should say that I was, in that first week, in a condition of some moral comfort. I had never carried a weapon in my life and I had now spent seven days doing nothing but arbitrating livestock, and a man can build a great deal out of two facts like that if he lays them side by side and does not look underneath either.

The goat was more complicated, and involved a genuine question of ownership, and I will admit that I decided it by working out which of the two claimants was lying, which took under a minute, because a man lying about a goat has the same face as a man lying about a stereo, and I have spent my life in rooms with the second one.

The circumcision I would rather not discuss. I was required to be present and to say something at the correct moment, and I said something, and it was fine, and I have never been able to eat anything sweet at that kind of gathering since.

By Thursday I had understood the shape of the job and the shape of the job was this: they did not want an answer. Almost nobody in the history of the world has ever wanted an answer. They wanted someone to be the person in the room who is not in it, and I had been the person in the room who is not in it since I was seventeen years old, from a stairwell, waiting for a family to go to bed.
I was, I am obliged to report, extremely good at this.
And on the Thursday afternoon, at the exact moment when I had begun — God forgive me, I had actually begun — to relax, a Peugeot came up the one road with a boy in it.
He got out with two bags of books and one bag of clothes, which tells you the whole story of Mojtaba Sadeghpour [moj-ta-BAA saa-DEGH-poor] and saves us both a great deal of time.

Nineteen. Four years in Qom [GHOM]. Sent to assist the new custodian of Emamzadeh Nur for a period of six months, at the request of nobody I could identify, on a form that had three stamps on it. He had a soft new beard that had cost him a great deal of anxiety and a way of standing perfectly straight while apologising.
He kissed my hand.
He said, "It's an honour, Sayyid. I've read almost nothing. I'm here to be useful."
And I looked at this child, with his two bags of books and his sincere and terrible eagerness, and I thought, with the clarity of a man watching a truck come towards him on a narrow road:
Ah. Here is my death, and it has brought luggage.
LESSON 9
A student is a witness who has volunteered.
He got me on the fourth day.

I had been careful. I had been so careful that I had developed a small repertoire of ailments — a throat, a headache, an obligation — which allowed me to hand him things. You lead it tonight, Mojtaba jan. It's good for them to hear a young voice. He glowed like a stove every time. It was the easiest management I have ever done and I was still going to lose, and I knew I was going to lose, and I was simply arranging the terms.
Then on the fourth evening, after the small night gathering, with the twelve regulars gone home and the two of us stacking the cushions, he said:
"Haj Aqa. May I ask about something you said."
I said, "You may always ask about something I said."
Which is a sentence I would like to have carved into a wall somewhere.

"On Tuesday. To the widow. You said —" and he quoted me, in Arabic, my own manufacture, back at me, perfectly, having heard it once. He has a memory like a wet floor: everything that walks across it leaves a print.
"I remember."
"I've looked for it."
"Have you."

"In four places." He was not accusing. That is what I want you to understand about Mojtaba. He was not accusing me of anything, he was worried on my behalf, he had spent his evening hunting through his own books trying to find a citation to protect his teacher from an error, and he had failed, and it was distressing him. "I can't find it, Sayyid. And I've looked in the places where I find everything."

Now. I had prepared for this. I had, in four separate sleepless hours, prepared eleven different answers to this question, and every single one of them was an attempt to make him wrong, and every single one of them would have worked once and then set him hunting for the rest of his life.
So instead I put down the cushion, and I looked at him for a while, and I said:
"No. You wouldn't."
He waited.
I did not fill it. Eleven seconds is a geological era, and I had learned in a mosque with two hundred and forty people in it that the silence gets attributed to whoever is standing more still.
Then I said, quite gently, "Mojtaba jan. Did it help her?"
"That isn't — Sayyid, forgive me, that isn't the question —"

"It isn't the question." I agreed with him warmly. I agreed with him so warmly and so completely that I appeared to have arrived at his position some years ago and continued on past it to somewhere with a better view. "You're quite right. It isn't the question. Sit down."
He sat down.
"Did it help her?"

And he opened his mouth, and closed it, and I watched a very intelligent nineteen-year-old discover that he could not say no without lying, because he had been there, he had seen the woman's face, and he had gone home that night and told his mother on the telephone that his new teacher was remarkable.
He said, "Yes."
I said, "Then we'll think about it."
We. I gave him the we. It cost me nothing and it turned an interrogation into a project, and a project is a thing a young man will carry for you for years.
He said, "Yes, Sayyid," and he stacked the last cushion and he went to bed.
And I want to record what happened next, because it is the true beginning of everything that went wrong, and it did not happen to me.

He lay in that room for a long time in the dark, on the other side of a wall with the damp in it, and he could not work out why he felt as if he had lost. He had been right. He had been demonstrably, textually, four-sources right, and the man had not even denied it, and somehow he had come away feeling like a boy who had brought a bus timetable to a funeral and read it out.
He was nineteen. He had four years of the finest scholastic training in the country and he had never once been in a room with a professional.
I heard him get up twice.
PART TWO — THE SMOKE
Lessons Ten to Eighteen
LESSON 10
Bless the kitchen. Nobody has ever blessed the kitchen.
There is a kitchen behind every shrine in this country and it is the only part of the operation that does anything.

Ours was a long room with two burners, a bank of pots the size of drums, and a cold store that had been a stable. Out of it came the food for every mourning gathering, every wedding, every Thursday night, and every stranger who came off that road at an inconvenient hour, which was all of them. Nine hundred people in Shurabad and I would estimate that six hundred of them had, at some point in their lives, eaten something at four in the morning that Shokouh made.

Nobody had ever mentioned it. Not once. In the whole apparatus — the dome, the silver, the trustees, the men in the courtyard discussing the tiles — there was no mechanism at all for noticing the kitchen. Twenty-two years she had been in it, six of them as a widow, and the arrangement was that food arrived and men said God be praised, and God, on this evidence, was doing the cooking.
So on the second Thursday I blessed it.

I want to be clear about my motives, since I am going to be judged on them and would prefer to be judged accurately. I did not do it out of justice. I did it because I had been in that town nineteen days and I had discovered that the only person in it who did not look at my hat was on her knees in a courtyard at five in the morning insulting a floor, and I had spent my entire adult life developing precisely one skill, and I now had a costume that forbade every application of it.

I could not touch her. I could not be alone with her. I could not compliment her, or look at her for longer than a sentence, or say a single one of the eleven things that had worked on every woman I had ever met since 1997.
But I could bless her kitchen.
I did it after the evening prayer, on the way out, in front of nine people, which is the correct dosage — a blessing given in private is a proposition, a blessing given in front of nine is a policy.

I stood in the doorway of that long room with the steam on the windows and I said that there is nothing in the House of God more sacred than the room where the food for the mourners is made. I said that a man who comes to a shrine to weep and is given tea has been answered, and that the answering was done in this room, by these hands, at an hour when the rest of us were asleep and congratulating ourselves on our devotion.
Then I gave them a hadith [ha-DEETH] — a saying handed down from the Prophet, one of the hundreds of thousands of them, each with a chain of names behind it going back to somebody who was there.

It was four clauses. It concerned the Prophet, peace be upon him, and a woman who fed the mourners of Uhud [o-HOD], and it contained the phrase she was not thanked in her lifetime, and this was noted, and it was, on every level available to scholarship, an invention.
It is now, I am told, embroidered on a cloth in a kitchen in Kashmar.

She was standing by the second burner with a colander in her hands. She had come out of the steam when I started and she had not moved since, and by the third clause her face had gone the colour of the inside of a fig, and by the fourth she had begun to look for somewhere to put the colander and had failed to find anywhere in the world.
The nine people said salavat, loudly, twice.
Then they filed out into the courtyard, and I stayed in the doorway, and she said, without looking up:
"Are you finished."
"No."
"God give me strength."
"There's a second part."
"There is not a second part."
"There's a second part about the water," I said.
"Haj Aqa." She put the colander down at last, upside down, on a wet surface, which is a thing she had not done in twenty-two years. "Get out of my kitchen."
I went out into the courtyard where the nine of them were waiting to tell me how moved they had been.
LESSON 11
Never answer a question you understand.
Mojtaba brought a book on the Sunday.

He had been building towards it for a week the way a boy builds towards asking his father for money. I watched him carry it around the shrine for two days without opening it, and on Sunday evening he set it down on the low table between us, squared it to the edge, and turned it so that it faced me.
It was a serious book. I knew that much. It had the binding they use for the ones you are not supposed to argue with, and there was a paper marker in it, and he had written on the marker.
He said, "Sayyid. About Uhud."
And I looked at the book.
I want to describe how I looked at the book, because it is the single most useful thing I have ever learned and I am handing it over now for nothing.

I did not look at Mojtaba. I looked at the book, and I let my face do the thing a man's face does when he sees an old friend across a road — a small softening around the eyes, a very slight movement of the head — and then I reached out and put two fingers on the cover, flat, the way you put your hand on a horse.
And I said nothing.
Forty seconds.

I have measured it since. I did it deliberately and I counted, and it was forty seconds, and I have never before or since sustained anything for forty seconds without moving. My hand on the cover. My eyes on the marker he had written. The stove ticking.
At about eighteen seconds he said, "I only meant —"
I raised my other hand very slightly off my knee, perhaps four centimetres, and put it down again.
He stopped.

At thirty-something seconds his eyes went to the door. That is the moment, if you are ever in this position, that you are waiting for: not the moment they doubt you, the moment they doubt the room. He had begun to feel that he had done something socially wrong. He could not have told you what. The book was a correct book. The marker was in the correct page. He had brought a legitimate scholarly instrument to a legitimate scholarly question, and somewhere in the last half-minute it had turned into a bus timetable that he was reading out loud at a funeral.
At forty I took my fingers off the cover and said:
"How is your mother?"
He said his mother was well.
"Does she know what you're doing here?"
He said his mother thought he was in Mashhad.

I let that sit for a while, because it was interesting, and because I had just discovered without asking that the boy's posting to Shurabad was not something he had told his family about, which meant that he had not chosen it, which meant that somebody had put him here. I filed it. It took me another six weeks to take the file back out.
Then I said, "Take the book with you. Read the whole chapter, not the page. Then we'll talk about Uhud."
He took the book and went out glowing, having been given homework, which to a certain kind of nineteen-year-old is the same as being kissed.

There are eleven pages in that chapter. I know because I counted them from the doorway, upside down, in the four seconds while he was gathering himself, which is a thing you learn to do reading account books off desks.

I have never read them. I could not have read them. But I knew there were eleven, and three weeks later I said, in front of him, to somebody else, there are eleven pages on it and not one of them settles the matter, and I watched the boy's whole face open like a window.
LESSON 12
Grief does not want an explanation. It wants a witness with good posture.
The first funeral I did was a woman of eighty-four who had died in her sleep, which everyone kept saying to me as though it were a legal finding they wanted upheld.

I was terrified. Not of the ritual — the ritual is choreography and I had the choreography by then. I was terrified of the house afterwards. In the mosque you are protected by the format. In the house they sit you in the corner by the window and they bring you tea and then the room slowly turns towards you and waits, and there is no format, and whatever comes out of your mouth in the next thirty seconds is the thing that family repeats to each other for forty years.
So I did what my mother did.

I should explain about my mother, and I will, properly, but the short of it is this: Parvaneh [par-vaa-NEH] could not read, and had opinions on everything, and when there was a death in our building she went and sat with the family, and she did not console them. That was the thing. She did not console anybody. She sat down and she said, Tell me about her hands, or Who did she like best, out of all of you, don't lie, and then she listened for two hours and remembered every name, and came back the next day and used them.
So in that house in Shurabad, in the corner by the window, with fourteen people waiting for a sayyid to say something about the mercy of God, I said:
"Which one of you did she prefer?"
There was a silence of a quality I had not heard before.

Then the middle daughter said, "Reza," and the room came apart — not into weeping, into argument, seven people at once, because it had not been Reza, it had obviously been Reza, it had been Reza only because he never visited and she liked a grievance, she had told the neighbour it was Reza to make Fatemeh jealous — and it went on for an hour and a half, and at one point a grandson was on his feet doing an impression of the old woman complaining about a saucepan, and everybody was crying, and everybody was laughing, and I sat in the corner and drank four glasses of tea and said perhaps twenty words in ninety minutes.
At the door the eldest son took both my hands and could not speak for a moment. Then he said, "Nobody has talked about her since
Tuesday. They've all been talking at us."

I went home along the wall of the shrine in the dark and I was not pleased with myself. That is the part I cannot make anybody believe. I was not pleased. I was disturbed, in a low, physical way, like a man who has picked up a familiar object and found it warm.

Because I had gone into that house intending to survive it. That was the entire plan. Survive the corner by the window, get out, twelve more days. And instead I had done my mother's trick, which is not a trick, which is the only thing she had, and it had worked, and fourteen people were now going to sleep better.
And I could not locate the con.

That is what disturbed me. I stood in the courtyard of Emamzadeh Nur at eleven o'clock at night and went through it the way you go through a job afterwards, looking for the seam — what did I take, what did they lose, where is the mark — and there was nothing there. Nobody had been taken. The transaction was clean.

I want to be very careful here, because this is the point at which people would like me to say that something opened in me. Nothing opened in me. What happened was smaller and, I think, worse. I had spent forty-six years operating a moral system with exactly two categories, and that night, for the first time, I met an act that fitted neither of them, and I did what any professional does with an object he cannot classify.
I put it in a drawer and did not look at it for two months.
LESSON 13
Attention is the only currency I ever counted correctly.

My father had a lock shop on a street off Nasser Khosrow, and he was the most devout crook I have ever known, and I include in that a man who used to say the traveller's prayer in the car on the way to a burglary.

He prayed five times a day for fifty-one years. He never missed the month of fasting, not once, not with pneumonia. He gave to beggars — actually gave, real money, in front of nobody, which is the test — and he cheated every single customer who ever came through his door. He sold a widow a lock in 1989 that he had bought in a job lot of four hundred, all with the same key, and he sold the other three hundred and ninety-nine in the same neighbourhood over the following decade.
I asked him about it once. I was eleven. I remember the tile I was standing on because it was cracked and I was working at it with my toe.

He looked at me with genuine bewilderment — that is the part that took me thirty years to understand, the bewilderment, he was not caught, he was not defensive, he simply could not locate my question — and he said:
"God asked me to pray. He did not ask me to charge fairly."
And then he went back to the bench.

He kept a ledger with God. Not on paper. In his head, and out loud, at dinner. Prayers on one side, transgressions on the other, and there were also credits available for things like being polite to his mother-in-law and not looking at the woman on the third floor. And by his own accounting, every night of his life, he was very slightly ahead.
He died ahead. I want that understood. He went out at seventy-one in profit.

My mother could not read and did not care to. She was a large loud woman who could carry a propane cylinder up four flights of stairs and did, weekly, and her name meant Butterfly, which she thought was the funniest thing that had ever happened to anyone.
Parvaneh burned esfand [es-FAND] for everything.

It is the little seed you buy in a paper cone from a child at the traffic lights. You put it on a coal and it goes off like tiny gunfire and makes a smoke that every Iranian on earth can identify blindfolded, and it turns away the evil eye. She burned it for exams and weddings, for a neighbour's new car, for my cousin's promotion, for illness, for a bad feeling on a Tuesday afternoon with no cause she could name. She burned it over me the day I started school and the day I was arrested and, I am told, the day I was born. When she thought someone had looked at me too admiringly at a wedding she would take me into the kitchen afterwards and do it over my head, going round three times, muttering, and I would stand there aged nine with my eyes shut being embarrassed.
I grew up inside that smoke. I could pick it out of a street at fifty metres.
I want you to hold onto this, because I did not. Four months I walked in and out of that shrine, and I want it on the record that I did not once — not once — think about my mother's kitchen.
And here is what she gave me, which is the only inheritance in this story.

She read rooms. She would walk into a family gathering and know inside four seconds who was pregnant, who was being cheated on, and who had lost money, and she would deliver her findings to me on the walk home like a man commentating a football match. Did you see the sister-in-law's hands? Empty. Nothing on them. And he's still buying pistachios for the neighbours — watch that, watch it, six months. She was right about the pistachios. She was right about everything, for forty years, in a two-room flat, with no education and no outlet and no possible use for any of it.
That is the whole of my professional training. My mother's parlour trick, applied to windows.

I married Mahnaz [mah-NAAZ] in 2003 and it lasted seven years. She knew what I did before the engagement and considered it a phase, like smoking, or communism. She was not naive. She simply had a theory about me that was more flattering than the evidence, and she held it for seven years with tremendous discipline, and when she finally put it down she did it in a single afternoon and never picked it up again, which I respected and which I have never recovered from.
We had a daughter in 2006. Golnar [gol-NAAR]. Pomegranate flower.

She was four when I left. She had a way of holding a spoon with her whole fist, like a weapon, and she narrated her food. Everything got a running commentary — the rice is going to the corner, the rice does not want to — and Mahnaz used to say, God help us, she's got your mouth, and I would laugh, because at that stage I still thought that was a good thing for a child to inherit.

That is all I am going to say about it here. It comes back. It comes back in a way I could not possibly have arranged and would not have dared to invent, and when it does I will tell it properly, and until then I would rather not.
LESSON 14
A woman who mocks you is doing you a courtesy.
Shokouh worked it out somewhere around the fifth week, and her response was to become, without warning and with terrible precision, the most pious woman in the province of Khorasan.

I understood immediately that I was being punished. What took me longer was the discovery that I could not do a single thing about it, because every weapon she used was a weapon I had put in her hand.
It began at the door of the cold store.

I had come to ask about the oil order. She was counting sacks. She turned round, saw me, and — with an expression of profound and reverent concern — took two steps backwards to a distance of about three metres, folded her hands, and looked at the floor.
"Haj Aqa."
"Shokouh khanum."
"Is this distance correct?" she said, to the floor. "I worry about the distance."
"The distance is —"
"Because I would hate," she said, "for there to be any question."
I said the oil was fine and left.

Then it was everything. For eleven weeks. She would call across a courtyard full of people: Haj Aqa, is it permitted to laugh on a Thursday? Only I laughed and then I thought, God forgive me, was that a Thursday. She would knock on my open door and ask, with enormous gravity, for a ruling on whether the cat was clean. She began, in front of witnesses, referring to me exclusively as His Excellency the Sayyid, in full, every time, with a small inclination of the head, until two of the older women started doing it as well and I had to hear it from them, sincerely, for the next four months.
The high point, and I concede it freely, was the ankle.

We were putting up the black cloth for the mourning nights, and she was on a chair, and the hem of her skirt moved perhaps two centimetres, and she froze, and turned her head very slowly, and said, in a voice of genuine ecclesiastical anxiety, loud enough for the entire courtyard:
"Haj Aqa. My ankle showed."
And I said something. I do not remember what. Something about the mercy of God being wide.
And she said, "You've gone a colour."

Now. I would like to explain what was actually happening in that courtyard, because a man reading this would be forgiven for thinking that a widow was tormenting a cleric, and that is the surface of it and the surface of it is a lie.
She was not tormenting a cleric. She had worked out that the cleric was not one.

Not the details — she had no route to the details, and would not have wanted them. What she had was a floor-washer's information, which is the best information in any building. She had watched me for five weeks and observed a man who did not know where anything was kept, who flinched at the word sanad [sa-NAD], which is the word for a deed, who had never once in five weeks corrected anybody's Arabic, and who listened — this was the tell, this was the thing that gave me away to exactly one person in nine hundred — who listened to her, at five in the morning, about a floor, with the full attention that men of that costume reserve for other men of that costume.
And she could not say any of that. There was no sentence available to her. A woman in Shurabad cannot walk up to the custodian of the shrine and say I don't think you're real.
So she did the only thing available, which was to take the costume itself and hold it up between us and shake it, over and over, in public, until we both had to look at it.
Every time she said Haj Aqa with that little full stop after it, she was saying: I can see the man in there. I am not going to tell anyone. Get out.
And I answered every one of them, and I answered them all wrong, on purpose, because I am a coward and it was the closest I had come to being spoken to in nine years.
I said: Yes. And I'm staying.
LESSON 15
Never be alone with what you want. Institute a committee.
The Thursday night recitation for the women of Shurabad was instituted in the eighth week and ran, I am told, for another nine years after I was gone.

I would like it recorded in the minutes that it was a considerable success. Attendance began at nine and stabilised at thirty-odd. Two women learned to read in it. A dispute between two families that had survived a wedding, a funeral and a court was settled in the third month by two grandmothers who found themselves seated on the same rug and could not, in that room, sustain it.
It was instituted so that I could be in a room with Shokouh Aramesh for forty minutes a week without committing a sin.
I want to walk through the engineering, because I am proud of it in the way a man is proud of a thing he should be ashamed of and has done extremely well.

I could not visit her. I could not walk with her. I could not send her anything, or receive anything, or say her name in a sentence with mine in it. In the entire architecture of that town there was no legal channel by which the custodian of the shrine and the woman who ran its kitchen could sit in the same room for any length of time without a reason.

So I built a reason. Thursday night, in the women's hall, a recitation and a short talk, open to all, tea afterwards — and the tea, obviously, from the kitchen, which meant the kitchen had to be represented, which meant Shokouh had to be in the room, which meant that for forty minutes every week I could look at the far wall and talk, and she would be somewhere to the left of it, and afterwards there would be a general noise of thirty women in which two people could exchange four sentences about crockery.
Four sentences. That was the yield. I built an institution for four sentences a week about crockery.
And here is the part that finished me, which I did not see coming and could not have priced.
I was good at it.

I do not mean the theology. There was no theology. I mean that thirty women came into a hall on a Thursday night and for the first time in the history of that shrine somebody stood in front of them and did not talk to them the way you talk to a school assembly. I asked things. My mother's things. Who did you learn it from — no, who actually, not who you're supposed to say. And they told me, and I remembered, and the next week I used their mothers' names, and by the fifth week there were thirty-two of them and a woman was coming in from a salt village nine kilometres out on the back of her son's motorcycle.
Shokouh sat at the back with the samovar and said nothing for eleven weeks.
Then in the twelfth, in the general noise, drying a glass, not looking at me, she said:
"You did that for me."
I said, "I did it for the crockery."
"Thirty-two women," she said. "You built a school for thirty-two women because you wanted to talk to me about a teapot."
"That is a very serious accusation."
"It is."
"You should take it to the trustee."
"Haj Aqa," she said, and put the glass down, and I have never in my life heard a full stop like it. "Do you know what the worst part is?"
I did not.
"It worked," she said. "For them. It actually worked for them."

And she picked up the samovar and carried it out, and I stood in an empty hall in the province of Khorasan holding a wet cloth, entirely alone, in the exact condition of a man who has been convicted of something and given a prize for it in the same sentence.
LESSON 16
Every priesthood is a trade with a uniform. That is not the scandal. That is the mercy.

In the third month I was summoned to Kashmar [kash-MAR] for two days of provincial meetings, and I went with my heart in my mouth expecting to be exposed by lunchtime on the first day, and instead I was very nearly bored to death.
There were about forty of us in a hall with a broken air conditioner. Here is what we discussed:

Stipend tiers. For four hours. There are grades, and the grades attach to your posting and your years and the size of the town, and the difference between the third and the fourth is enough to matter if you have a daughter getting married, and about eleven men had a daughter getting married, and they had the figures memorised the way men in my trade memorise the response time of a district.
Then: the housing allowance and whether the shrine house counts against it. Then: a very long dispute about a form.
I sat at the back and did the only thing I know how to do, which is watch.
They were civil servants.
I want to say this carefully because it is the closest thing to a discovery that I made in that entire year, and everyone I have ever told it to has heard the opposite of what I said.

I had come in expecting a conspiracy. I am a criminal; I understand conspiracies; I would have known exactly what to do inside one. And what I found in that hall was forty men in their fifties with bad backs, on a wage that would not embarrass a bus inspector, arguing about a form.

There was a man from a village east of us who had washed corpses for thirty-one years. He had a routine about it. He did it at the tea break with four of us leaning on a wall and it was, I am not exaggerating, better material than most of what you will hear from professionals — the ones who float, and why, and what the families say, and a passage about a man who had been a very great bully in life and required, in death, four people to hold him down. He did that bit twice because we asked him to. He was funny the way a surgeon is funny.
And then somebody asked after his wife and he said she had been gone two years and he was managing, and everybody looked at their tea.

There was a man of about sixty who told me, unprompted, in a corridor, in the flattest voice imaginable, that he had not believed in any of it for twenty years. He said it the way you would mention a knee. I said — and it came out before I could route it — then why? And he said that there were eleven hundred people in his district and somebody had to bury their mothers properly, and if he went, they would send a boy from Qom who would do it correctly and coldly, and he was not prepared to hand those families over to a boy from Qom.
Then he asked me if I had any tobacco.

There were careerists. Obviously there were careerists. Three or four of them, smooth, in good cloth, with the Qom accent laid over something else, and my whole skin went up when they came into the room, because I have spent my life in rooms with crews and I know a crew when I see one at a distance of forty metres. They were doing something. I never found out what. It had nothing to do with God and everything to do with a cement plant.

And there were two men in that hall — I will not name them, one is still alive — of such plain and unadvertised decency that I found it physically difficult to stand near them. One of them helped me with a form for eleven minutes. He had no idea who I was and he will never know and he was simply a man who could see that somebody was struggling with a form.
I came out of Kashmar with something worse than the conspiracy I had gone in expecting.

Because if it had been a conspiracy, I could have despised it and gone on wearing the coat with a clear conscience. Instead it was a profession — a badly paid, badly run, mostly sincere profession with rot running through the middle of it, and the decent men knew about the rot, and knew about the cement, and they stayed anyway, because leaving would hand eleven hundred families to somebody worse.
I sat on the bus back to Shurabad and worked out, somewhere around the salt flat, that I had spent two days among men who had made exactly my decision.
The difference between us was a piece of paper and thirteen centuries.

I have thought about this more than is healthy. The conclusion I reached that night is the one I still hold, and it is not the comfortable one and it is not the cynical one either, which is why nobody likes it:

Every priesthood on earth is a trade with a uniform. So is every court, and every hospital, and every police force. The uniform is not a fraud perpetrated on the public — the uniform is a device that allows an ordinary man with a bad back to walk into the worst hour of a stranger's life and be useful there, which no ordinary man can do on his own authority, because on his own authority nobody would let him in the door.
The uniform is the mercy. It is also the crime. It is the same object.
I was, at that point, the only man in the province wearing one that fitted.
LESSON 17
The tray.
There was a tray.
It was Thursday, late, in the passage outside the women's hall, and the tray was on the low shelf where it always was, and we both reached for it at the same time.
Her hand was on the left handle. Mine was on the right.
Nothing happened.

We stood there, either side of a brass tray with eleven glasses on it, in a passage with a bulb that had been going for a month, and nothing happened for a period of time I am not able to state accurately because I stopped counting, which I have never otherwise done in my life.

I could hear the samovar in the hall behind her. I could hear a woman laughing at something. I could hear, very distinctly, the noise the salt makes in the walls at night, which is a thing you stop hearing after a week and which I heard then.
She did not look up and I did not look down.
Her thumb was on the brass. There was a burn scar across the base of it, old, from a pan, and I had known about that scar for eleven weeks and had never once been in a position to look at it.
Then she said, "Let go."
And I let go.

And she picked up the tray with both hands and carried it into the hall, and I stood in the passage for a while longer, and then I went and prayed the night prayer with two hundred people and did not remember one second of it.
LESSON 18
If God speaks to you, be polite. If He does not, be quicker.
Now I have to tell you about the chamber, and I would rather not, and I have never done it well.

Underneath the blue dome of Emamzadeh Nur there is an inner room. It is not large — four paces by five — and it is old, much older than the dome, low enough that a tall man must attend to his head. The grave is in the middle under a lattice of wood and silver. The walls are stone and there is one door and there is no window.

There was a vent. High on the north wall. It was bricked up in 1961, and I noticed the brick in my second week, and thought nothing of it, because a man notices bricks the way a butcher notices a limp.

Three nights a year, in the mourning season, the chamber is opened for the vigil. People come off the road from four provinces. They arrive having fasted since dawn, most of them having travelled overnight on a bus, many of them for a specific reason — a sick child, a court case, a father — and they sit in that room in the dark from the night prayer until first light.
And the braziers are lit.

Esfand. Sacks of it. Not a pinch on a coal in a kitchen doorway — sacks, in four braziers, replenished by two men in rotation, for eight hours, in a stone room four paces by five with one door and no vent.
I had been in that room during the day. I had not been in it during the vigil.

Haj Rasoul took me in himself at ten o'clock at night on the second night, with his hand under my elbow, and he said, "You'll want to sit at the north wall, Sayyid. Under the brick. It's easier there."
I have gone over that sentence for twenty years.

There were perhaps sixty people in the chamber. The smoke was not a haze. I want to be exact, because everyone who has not been in that room imagines a haze, and it was not a haze, it was a substance — you could see the shape of your own breath going into it and not coming back. The heat off four braziers in a stone box. And the sound, which I had not anticipated at all: sixty people in the dark, none of them speaking, breathing.
The first two hours were nothing. That is important. Nothing happened for two hours except that I became aware of my own eyelids.

Then the walls began to move, and I would like to describe this precisely, because it was not that they appeared to move. I have had a fever. That is not what this was. The stone breathed in and out, slowly and with enormous patience, and the correct thing to say about it was not the wall seems to be moving but the wall has always been doing this and you have simply never been quiet enough to notice, and I understood, sitting there, that I had been wrong about the nature of stone for forty-six years and had now been corrected.
Then time came apart.

Not sped up. Not slowed. Came apart — into pieces that did not have to be in order, so that a thing that had happened in 1991 was available in the room, adjacent to me, and I could go and look at it. I went and looked at several. I went and looked at my father's bench. I went and looked at a stairwell in Karaj.

And the geometry started, which I cannot do anything with in words. Behind my eyes and also on the wall, which were the same place. Patterns, moving, endlessly generating and folding, and none of it random — that was the thing about it, the offensive thing, it was so obviously designed that the design felt like an argument being made to me personally by somebody with a great deal more time than I had.
Around the fourth hour I understood that I was not alone in the room, and I do not mean the sixty people.
There was an attention on me.

I have been watched by police. I know what being watched feels like from every angle and every distance and I am telling you that this was not that and it was not imagination either, and if you want to say it was chemistry then I agree with you completely and it does not help me at all, because I was there and the chemistry was extremely specific about who it was.
It knew me.
And it addressed me — not in a voice, there was no voice, there was a fact that arrived the way a fact arrives when you remember your own telephone number — and what arrived was:
Panjshanbeh.

Nobody in Shurabad knew that name. Nobody within four hundred kilometres of that room knew that name. It had been said out loud perhaps two hundred times in a prison block by men who were now dead or elsewhere, and it arrived in that chamber like a bill.
And my mouth — because I have exactly one register under pressure, and it is not awe —
I said, out loud, in a stone room with sixty mourners in it:
"Oh, don't."
Somebody near me shifted.
You have been brought back, said the fact.
"Back."
You were here.

"I have never been here in my life," I said, out loud, to a wall, "I have never been east of Mashhad, and if You're going to do this at least do it to somebody who deserves it, because I am extremely busy —"
She stood where you are sitting.

And the geometry did something then that I will not attempt, and I saw a queue. A queue of women, along a wall, in daylight, in clothes from before I was born, and it was not a vision in the sense that I saw it, it was more that I was informed of it with total authority, and one of them was near the front, and she was young, and she was large and loud and she was carrying something, and I knew her, and I have never been able to decide since whether I recognised her face or was simply told to.
I said, "That's not fair."

And the fact did not answer, because it had said what it had, and it went, and the room came back a piece at a time over about ninety minutes, and at some point in there I was crying, in the dark, in a black turban, in a room full of people who were all doing the same thing and none of whom found it remarkable.
At first light two men carried the braziers out and opened the door and the cold came in like water.
Haj Rasoul was in the courtyard with a glass of tea for me, standing exactly where he had been standing eight hours earlier, looking extremely well rested.
He said, "It's something, isn't it."
I said it was something.
"Every year," he said, "every year I think, this year I'll be ready for it." He laughed, the door-in-a-draught laugh. "You're pale, Sayyid. Sit. Sit. Drink that."

I sat on the step and drank the tea, and my hands were not steady, and I thought — and this is the last coherent thought I had before I slept for eleven hours — I have to find out what my mother was doing in this town.

Which is when a girl came in through the gate off the morning bus, with a plastic folder under her arm, and asked the man sweeping the courtyard whether this was where the sayyid was who signs things.
PART THREE — THE LEDGER
Lessons Nineteen to Twenty-Seven
LESSON 19
Nobody looks at a cleric's face.

I slept eleven hours and came out into the courtyard at four in the afternoon with my head full of wool, and Mojtaba said there was a girl waiting who had been waiting since morning and had refused three separate offers of food.
"From where?"
"Tehran, Sayyid. She came on the morning bus. She has a folder."

They all have a folder. I had learned by then that the folder is the whole personality of the visit — a thin folder is a man who wants a favour, a fat folder is a man who has been to eleven offices and has stopped believing in any of them.

She was in the courtyard by the tap, on the low wall, with a plastic document wallet on her knees, and she stood up when I came out of the passage, and the first thing I registered was that she stood up wrong. Everyone in Shurabad stands up for the coat in a particular way — hands, eyes down, a half-bow that continues for a moment after it should stop. She stood up the way you stand up for a doctor who is running late.
Tehran. Obviously Tehran. Cheap coat, good shoes, a face that had been in eleven waiting rooms in five weeks and had run entirely out of the resource that makes people polite in waiting rooms.
She was perhaps nineteen.
She said, "Are you the one who signs things?"
And I said something. I have no idea what.
Then Mojtaba, at my shoulder, doing his job beautifully, said, "The lady's name is —"
And she said it herself, over him, flatly, in the way of a person who has said it at eleven counters and has learned to get it in first:
"Golnar Fani."
I want to tell you what I did, and it is nothing, and it is the finest professional performance of my life.

I have sat in stairwells for four hours. I once stood in a stranger's hallway for ninety seconds while the owner searched the room I had just come out of. I have a body that does not report to me under pressure and I have always been grateful for it in the way you are grateful for a good tenant.
I said, "Come in out of the sun."

That is all. There is nothing else in the record. My face did not move, my hands did not move, my voice did the slow thing it does. Mojtaba, who watched me every hour of every day for nine months and who noticed everything, noticed nothing.

We went into the office, which is a room with a desk and two chairs and a picture of a martyr from a town nearby, and she sat down and put the folder on the desk and squared it, and I sat down opposite my daughter for the first time in fifteen years.
She did not know me.
I want to be very careful about this, because it is the exact place where everything I had been saying about my hat stopped being a joke.

I was thirty-one when she last saw me properly. I was clean-shaven, and thin, and I wore reading glasses I did not need, and I smelt of cigarettes and a cologne she would probably still recognise on a stranger in a lift. I am forty-six now. I have a beard that took nine months. I had lost eleven kilos in Vakilabad and put six back on Shokouh's rice.

But that is not why she did not know me. Let us not pretend. A daughter knows her father across a road at forty metres in the dark; there are people in this country who have identified a man from the back of his neck after twenty years.
She did not know me because I was wearing a black turban, and nobody looks at a cleric's face.

You look at the hat. Then you look at your own hands, because you are about to ask for something, and because you were taught at seven that it is not correct to look. In nine months in Shurabad I had been looked at, properly, in the face, by three people: Shokouh Aramesh, Mojtaba Sadeghpour, and a four-year-old at a wedding who was subsequently removed.
I had spent my entire adult life becoming invisible by putting on reading glasses.
And I had finally achieved it by putting on the one object in the country that every single person in the room is guaranteed to be looking at.
LESSON 20
A document is a wall with a door in it, and the door is a person.
Here is what she wanted.

She was getting married.
