To do that, a woman in this country needs her father's permission, and her father was unavailable, and had been unavailable for six years in a way that was not legally the same as being dead. Her mother's position — delivered, I could hear it in the way Golnar reported it, in the tone you use about an earring that went down a drain — was that he was probably dead. The court's position was that probably is not a document.

So she needed the court to declare him absent. To get that she needed a file, and the file needed things in it — dates, the last known address, a statement of the efforts made — and the clerk at the court in Tehran had looked at her file five weeks ago and told her it was thin.
She had then been to eleven offices.
And somewhere in the eleventh, a woman in a queue had told her about a place out past Kashmar where the sayyid signs things.
That is the sentence. That is how my daughter came to be sitting across a desk from me.

Not a miracle. Not the hand of God, though I am obliged to concede that if the hand of God were involved it would have arranged it exactly this way, being a great enthusiast for the ironic route. She came because Haj Rasoul Sarmadi had spent four decades cultivating a reputation for our shrine — they'll help you there, they don't ask, they don't charge — and he had cultivated it deliberately, because a shrine that solves paperwork is a shrine that people come to, and people who come to a shrine leave something in the tin.
The corruption of the institution delivered my daughter to my door. There is no other mechanism in the story. It was not repentance that brought her and it was not grace. It was the pilgrim trade.
"What do you actually need from me?"
"A statement," she said. "That I came here. That I asked. That I'm not — " she looked for the word and did not find a polite one — "that I'm not doing this to get rid of him."
"And are you?"
She looked up.
That was the first time she looked at my face, and it lasted about a second, and I did not enjoy it.
"No," she said. "I'd like him to turn up at the wedding and be humiliated. But I can't put that on a form."
I said, "No. Most of the true things don't go on the form."
And she laughed — one syllable, out of the nose, entirely without pleasure, exactly the way I laugh — and said, "Are you going to be like this the whole time?"
LESSON 21
When you cannot say no, say yes at a length nobody can survive.
I could not sign it.
Every route out of that room ended with her leaving Shurabad on the evening bus, and I had eleven minutes to build something that would keep her in it.

Consider my position. If I signed the thing that afternoon she would take it, thank me, catch the six o'clock, and I would have had my daughter in a room for ninety minutes at the age of nineteen and would then have gone back to blessing kitchens.
So I invented a procedure.

I said that in a matter of this kind — the declaration of absence of a living man, which is not a small thing, which touches the standing of a family — the shrine could not simply issue a paper. There was a form to it. There was a period.
"A period."
"Forty days," I said, "is customary."
She said, "Forty days?"
"Forty is the customary number."

Now, this is true. Forty is the customary number in this country for absolutely everything. Forty days of mourning, forty days of chelleh [chel-LEH] in the winter, forty days of anything a man wishes to make sound both ancient and non-negotiable. It is the great load-bearing integer of Persian life and I want to say publicly that I have never in my life encountered a smoother instrument. Say forty to an Iranian and some part of him lies down.
She said, "I've got a wedding in Ordibehesht [or-dee-beh-HESHT]."

"Then we shall write to the court," I said, "and inform them that the matter is under examination at the shrine, which will hold your file open, and the clerk will have something to put in his hand, which is what a clerk is for."
She looked at me for a long moment.
"You know what a clerk is for," she said.
"I have been to offices."
"Sayyids don't usually know what a clerk is for."
I said, in the slow voice, "I was not always this."
Which is the single most honest sentence I spoke in nine months, and she took it as modesty about a seminary education, and thanked me for it.
The forty days had a rider, which I produced at the door, as an afterthought, because everything important is produced at the door as an afterthought.
"You'll need to come back at the end of it," I said. "In person. Once. It cannot be posted. The declaration has to be witnessed at the shrine."

None of this exists. I want to be absolutely clear, for the record and for the boy this is written for: none of it exists, not one clause, not the forty days, not the witnessing, not the letter to the court. I made an entire canonical procedure out of the air in a room in Shurabad at half past four in the afternoon, and I did it to buy six weeks.
It is still in use.

I heard about it four years later, in a completely different province, from a man who described it to me in some detail, with a small correction to my version which he said was the older and more correct form.
LESSON 22
Let them do the material. Nod at the punchlines.

She stayed four days on that first visit, in the women's guest room behind the kitchen, because the evening bus does not exist on a Wednesday and because Shokouh took one look at her and made a decision.
And on the second evening, in the office, with the tea going cold, my daughter did nine minutes on me.

I need to explain that she had a routine. Not a grievance — a routine, worked up over years, with a running order and callbacks, the kind of thing you develop when you are fourteen and discover that if you get to the subject before anybody else does you control the entire room. She had performed it at parties. You could hear the polish on it.
It opened with the reading glasses.

"He didn't need them," she said. "My mother told me. Twenty-something years, glasses, perfect eyesight. He thought they made him look like a man with an appointment." A beat. She had a beat. "He was a burglar. He'd put on glasses to go and rob a flat. In case somebody thought he wasn't serious."
I said, "Ah."
"So that's the level."
"Mm."

Then she did the Thursdays. She did the Thursdays for two full minutes — the working week of a man who only committed crimes on a Thursday, out of respect for the weekend, and who declined to work Fridays out of consideration for a God he did not believe in, in case it was rude. She had a whole passage about him having a better work-life balance than her mother's second husband.
I made a small sympathetic noise.

Then the knocking, which she did not know was true and which is the only part of the whole nine minutes I would have disputed. Then the arrest, which she did briskly, because the arrest is not funny and she knew it — except for one line, which she delivered flat, into the glass, and which went through me like a nail: "He never carried a weapon. That's the thing. That's what he'd want on the stone. He never carried a weapon." Then the years of the postcards, which I had not known about and which she attributed to me and which must have been my mother, and I sat there and let a woman thank my mother's ghost by mocking me.
And the closer — she landed it, she really did land it — was the photograph.

"He kept a photograph of me," she said. "That's the story. That's what my aunt tells everybody, this big tragic thing, he carries her photograph." She turned her glass around on the desk. "I was four in it. Four. He's had fifteen years to get an updated one. There's a photograph of me on my mother's cousin's Instagram that eleven thousand people have seen." A beat. "He could have looked at that. It's free."
Nine minutes. Callbacks in it. Genuinely, professionally funny.

And I sat opposite her in a black turban with my hands folded and I nodded gravely, and made the small sympathetic noise at the punchlines, and once, when she got to the glasses, I said, "Ah — the poor man," and she said, "Poor man," and did another thirty seconds she had clearly not planned, which were the best thirty seconds of the whole thing.
At one point I laughed.

Out loud, properly, at a joke my daughter made about me, in front of her, and she was delighted, because nobody had ever laughed at the material in a shrine before, and she said, "Sorry, Haj Aqa, I shouldn't —" and I said, "No. No. It's very good."

It was very good. That is the part I have never been able to explain to anybody. It was very good. She had my mouth, exactly as Mahnaz predicted, and she had taken the single worst thing that ever happened to her and made nine tight minutes out of it, and my professional assessment — I am not able to give you any other kind — was that she had done a better job with the material than I had.
Then the tea was finished and she said, "God, I'm sorry. You must get this all day."
"I do."
"Do you ever want to just tell people to grow up?"
And I said, "Every hour."
LESSON 23
If you must invent scripture, invent it against yourself.
On the fourth morning, an hour before the bus, she stopped performing.
It happened at the tap in the courtyard, without preamble, the way the real ones always do — she was rinsing a glass and she said, to the wall:
"Can I ask you something as a — " she made a small gesture at my hat — "as that."
"Yes."
"Am I allowed to hate him?"
I said nothing, which by then was not a technique.

"Because everybody has an opinion," she said. "Everybody. My mother says forget him, my aunt says he's still your father, the man I'm marrying says it's not healthy — they've all got a position." She put the glass down. "And they all want me to arrive somewhere. Forgive him, or get past it, or use it, or write him a letter I don't send. There's always a destination."
"And you don't want to go anywhere."

"I want to know if I'm permitted." She looked up, and this time it was not a second, it was much longer, and she was looking straight into my face and finding a cleric in it. "Not whether it's good for me. Whether it's allowed. Because if it's allowed then I can just — hate him. Quietly. Forever. And go and have a life. And nobody has to say anything else about it."
Now.
I had eleven months of practice by that point and I could produce four clauses of Arabic in the time it takes most men to clear their throat. I had a stock. I had, God help me, favourites.

And I stood in that courtyard and I understood with total clarity that if I gave her stock, she would take it, and it would be the answer she carried for the rest of her life, and it would be worth nothing, and I would have robbed her in a way that would have made my father blink.
So I took a long time.
I sat down on the low wall by the tap and I put my hands on my knees and I said, "Sit down."

And then I made it. Right there. In front of her, out of nothing, the way I had made everything else in that town, except that this one I made slowly and I made it well, and I have never worked harder on anything in my life, before or since, than I worked on four clauses of counterfeit Arabic in a courtyard in Shurabad in the eleven minutes before a bus.
I said it first. The whole thing, low, in the cadence, four clauses, the long vowel in the third position.
Then — and I had never done this, not once in nine months — I translated it.

I said: The hatred of the wronged is not a debt they owe. It is a wall the wrongdoer built, and it stands on his ground, and he pays the rent on it. She is not required to pull it down. She is required only to build her house somewhere else, and not against it.
She did not say anything for a while.
Then she said, "Is that real?"
And I said, "It's older than both of us."

Which was, at that moment, the largest lie I had told in my entire life, and also — I have thought about this for twenty years and I still hold it — the only true thing I ever said in that costume, because the sentence was correct. It is correct. I have tested it against everything since and it holds.

She got out her telephone and asked me to say it again so she could write it down, and I said it again, slowly, and she wrote it in Persian in the notes application with her thumbs, and asked me twice about a word.
And then she got on the bus.

And I stood in the courtyard of Emamzadeh Nur at ten past nine in the morning having invented a verse of scripture which gave my daughter formal religious permission to hate me for the rest of her life, and having watched her receive it with enormous relief and thank me for it, and having watched her thumbs.
I went inside and sat down and I did not move for about an hour.
Shokouh came in at some point and looked at me and went out again and did not ask, and that was the first indication I had that I was in serious trouble.
LESSON 24
A woman who can measure you by eye has already done it.
My abaya went at the shoulder in the eleventh month, which is what happens to a garment worn every day by a man who has never once had to take care of a garment.

Shokouh announced that she would make another. She announced it to the kitchen, at volume, in the third person — His Excellency the Sayyid will not be doing the rounds in Kashmar looking like a scarecrow — and I said that this was not necessary, and everybody in the kitchen laughed at me.
Measuring a man you cannot touch is a technical problem and she solved it in the courtyard on a Tuesday in front of four witnesses, which is the correct dosage.
She stood four feet away with a notebook and she looked at me.
"Turn."
I turned.
"Not like that. Slowly. Like the world's slowest — yes. There."

Four witnesses. Two of them were the older women who had started calling me His Excellency in earnest. One was Mojtaba, who was holding the notebook and had been told to write down numbers he did not understand and was doing it with tremendous seriousness.

She narrated. That was the method. She walked around me at a distance of four feet, entirely legal, entirely proper, not once within a metre, and she said the numbers out loud for the boy to write down, and the numbers were the least of it.

"Shoulder to floor — one forty-eight. He's got one shoulder lower than the other. Write that. The left. It's from carrying something for years, that. Sleeve — write sixty-two, and then write sixty-one, because he does this with his wrists." She did it. She did an impression of my hands. It was accurate. "Chest, he's lost weight this month, don't argue, I know what goes back to the kitchen. Neck — " a pause of exactly the wrong length — "the neck's fine."
I stood in the middle of a courtyard in the province of Khorasan and was read out loud to four people for six minutes.

I have been in a courtroom. I have stood while a judge in Mashhad went through my life at some length and gave me twelve years. I was more comfortable in that room than I was in that courtyard, and the difference is that the judge did not know about my wrists.
At the end she shut the notebook and said, "Well. He's not a difficult shape."
"Thank you."
"It wasn't a compliment. Difficult shapes are interesting."

And the four witnesses laughed and went off to tell everybody, and the story got around Shurabad within a day as further evidence of the delightful informality of the new sayyid, who lets the kitchen speak to him like that, God bless him, he's not proud.
Here is what I did not see until much later, and it happened during the ankle-length silence.
Golnar had been gone eight days.

And while Shokouh was doing the thing with the wrists, one of the older women said — as a pleasantry, filler, the sort of noise you make in a courtyard — "That girl who came, was she any relation? She had your way of turning her head."
And I said, "No. No relation."
And I said it correctly. My voice did the slow thing. My hands did nothing. It was, again, a flawless piece of work.
And Shokouh Aramesh, who was four feet away with a notebook and who had spent eleven months in a room with me, did not look up, and wrote something down, and went to the kitchen.
I found out much later that what she wrote down was 61.
She had already written 61.

A shrine is a business with a saint on the letterhead. Read the books.

The ledgers of Emamzadeh Nur went back to 1938 and were kept in a cupboard in the office, and in the eleventh month I read them, all of them, over nine nights, because I was avoiding thinking about my daughter and because a man's vices come back to him under stress.
I read them the way I used to read account books off a desk in the dark: not for the numbers, for the shape.
Here is the shape.

The shrine takes in more money than a shrine of that size, in a town of nine hundred at the end of a road, has any business taking in. Not a fortune. Nobody was building anything. But the pilgrim volume was wrong — three nights a year in the mourning season the town takes in four provinces' worth of people, and the tin fills, and the tin has filled, in the same pattern, since before the war with Iraq.

And the reputation was doing it. Emamzadeh Nur, out past Kashmar. People see things there. Not a rumour the trustees denied. Not a rumour they advertised either, which is much more expensive and much more effective.
Second thing. The trustee family. Sarmadi, four generations, uninterrupted since 1911. That is not unusual in itself.
Third thing, and this is where I stopped being a man passing an evening.
The register of custodians.

The custodian is not the trustee. The trustee is local and hereditary and runs the money. The custodian is the cleric, sent in, appointed, the man in the coat. And in that register, going back to 1938, there were nineteen of them.
Nineteen custodians in eighty-seven years. The longest served nine years. The average was closer to four. And every one of them left in the same three ways: transferred, returned to Qom, or a blank.
Nobody stays. That was the shape. Nobody stays in Shurabad, and everybody in Shurabad stays forever.
I went back to the entry for my predecessor.
Sayyid Hadi Vahedi [saa-YED HAA-dee vaa-heh-DEE]. Appointed the previous spring. And beside his name, in the column, in Haj Rasoul's handwriting: transferred, Mashhad.
Dated four weeks before I got off the bus.

Now. I had lived eleven days of somebody else's mail by then and I had never once asked a question about the man whose coat I was wearing, because it had not been in my interest to, and because there is a discipline to this and the discipline is do not look under the thing you are standing on.

But I had been in a hospital in Mashhad. I had seen him. He was on a gurney in a pre-operative bay with his hands arranged on his chest by somebody who had cared enough to arrange them, and he was sixty-five, and he was dead, and the date on the transfer was four weeks before.
A man does not get transferred to Mashhad and then die in a hospital there four weeks later with his post still being met at a bus stop for eleven consecutive nights.
Unless the transfer is the paperwork you write afterwards.
I sat in that office at two o'clock in the morning with the ledger open and I did the thing I have done all my life, which is not panic, which is inventory. And the inventory came out like this:
The vacancy I walked into was not a vacancy. It was made.

And the eleven nights of meeting the bus were not eleven nights of hope. I closed the ledger. I put it back in the cupboard, third from the left, spine out, the way I had found it.
Then I went and stood in the courtyard for a while and looked at the dome, and thought about the fact that I had been shown the cash tin on my first night by a man who was counting it.
He had not been testing whether I would steal.
He had been testing whether I was a professional.

I have entered the tradition. I have contributed.

It was a wedding I had no business at, four hours away, and I was in a room of about sixty men, and a cleric I had never met — decent, tired, sixty, one of the corridor men, a man with a knee — stood up to say the words over the food.
And he said mine.
The Uhud one. The woman who fed the mourners. She was not thanked in her lifetime, and this was noted.

Word perfect. Better than word perfect — he had improved the third clause. He had done something to the rhythm of it that I had not been good enough to do, and it landed harder, and sixty men said salavat.

And he said, with the absolute confidence of a man who has been doing this for thirty years, that it was well known, and that he had it from a teacher in Neyshabur [ney-shaa-BOOR], and that there was some dispute about the chain but the meaning was sound.
Some dispute about the chain but the meaning was sound.
I had made it up eleven months earlier standing in a doorway looking at a woman holding a colander.
I went out into the yard and stood by a wall. There were fairy lights in a tree and a generator going, and I stood there in my new abaya with my lower shoulder and I did the arithmetic.
Eleven months. Perhaps forty inventions, of which maybe nine had legs. A shrine that takes four provinces three nights a year. Men from those four provinces going home and using what they heard.
I was in the water supply.
And then the thought that has kept me up more nights than the dead man, the ledger, and the girl combined:
Are mine working better?

Because they were. I want to be careful. I am not saying they were better — I have no standing to say anything about better, I cannot read four words in a row. And I knew exactly why, and the reason is humiliating and simple: I made mine in response to a specific person in a specific room with a specific injury, at the moment of the injury, with no obligation to be true.
The real ones had to survive thirteen centuries and four schools of law and a war. Mine had to get one woman through a Tuesday.
Of course mine landed.

So which of these two facts is the scandal? That a thief was manufacturing scripture in the province of Khorasan and it was going into the water? Or that it fitted, that it went in without a ripple, that a tradition thirteen centuries deep took a fake from a man in the wrong shoes and improved the rhythm of it and passed it on with a note about the chain?
I have an answer. It is the wrong answer and I have never been able to get rid of it: neither.

Neither is the scandal. The scandal is that this is how it has always worked, that every one of those thirteen centuries was made of men in rooms with people who were suffering, saying the thing that would land, and the ones that landed got carried, and after enough carrying nobody can tell any more, and — here is the part I cannot put down — it does not matter, because the woman in the kitchen in Kashmar with the cloth on the wall is not being lied to. She is being told that her work was noticed. Which is true. Which was always true, and which nobody had said out loud for twenty-two years because there was no mechanism.
I made a mechanism.
I made it for a bad reason, out of nothing, to impress a widow.
I got back into the car and told the driver it had been a lovely wedding.

A student who cannot convict you will acquit the whole world instead.
Mojtaba came to me in the twelfth month with fourteen pages.

He had been quiet for a fortnight — not sullen, working, the lamp on in his room until two, and I had assumed with a kind of resigned calm that he was building the case. Fourteen pages is a case. I had been ready for it since the fourth day.

He put them on the low table and squared them to the edge and turned them to face me, exactly as he had turned the book, eleven months earlier, and I felt something in my chest that was almost affection for the both of us.
And then he did not accuse me of anything.
What he had written was an argument.
I want to state what was in it as accurately as I can, because he was nineteen and because it was better than anything I could have built, and because it destroyed his life.

He began from the observed facts, which he set out without comment, and which were: that in eleven months he had been unable to verify a single citation of mine in any of the four collections available to him; that he had written to a friend in Qom on a pretext and received back nothing; that certain of my chains were not merely unattested but structurally impossible, involving men who were dead before other men were born, and he gave two examples, both correct, both mine, and I had to look at the ceiling.

He then set out the second column of facts. The rate of resolution of disputes in Shurabad, which he had counted. The attendance of the women's Thursday. Two names — I will not write them — of people in that town who had been in a bad way and were not now. He had counted things. Nobody had asked him to count anything.
And then, on page nine, he asked his question, and his question was not is my teacher a fraud.
His question was: what is the text for?

He proposed — carefully, with a great deal of it may be that I am mistaken — that a chain of transmission is not the thing itself. That it is a device for carrying the thing across time, and that the thing being carried is the answering of a person in front of you. And that a man who can answer the person in front of him without the device is not standing outside the tradition. He is standing where the tradition was standing when it was young, before anybody had needed to write anything down, because nobody had died yet.
He wrote, on page eleven, a sentence I have carried for twenty years:
The isnad [es-NAAD] is a rope thrown to a man who cannot swim. It is not a criticism of the water.
Nineteen years old. In a damp room in a salt town. On his own.
He looked up at me when I had finished and his face was — I have to say it — hopeful. He was not accusing me. He was showing his teacher a piece of work.
And I understood, sitting there, several things at once.

The first was that he knew. Not the whole of it — he had not got to the hospital or the chair or the shoes, and he was not going to, not from me. But he knew the load-bearing part, which is that the man in front of him was not producing the tradition, and he had decided it did not matter, and he had built fourteen pages of scaffolding to hold that decision up.

The second was that the scaffolding was good. That was the horror. If it had been sophistry I could have taken it apart and sent him back to Qom with a fright and a clean conscience. It was not sophistry. It was an argument, and I have watched it hold up against much better men than me, later, in worse rooms.
The third was that he had done to himself, at nineteen, on paper, exactly what I had done to myself in Kashmar on a bus: he had looked at the machine, and seen the rot, and stayed.

I could have ended it there. That is the thing I want on the record, since everything after this is my fault and I would like the fault entered at the correct date. I could have said, Mojtaba, burn this, go home, your mother thinks you're in Mashhad. Four seconds. He would have gone.
What I said was:
"Page eleven is the whole thing. The rest is you being frightened of page eleven."
And he went red to the ears with happiness.
And I sent a boy of nineteen out of that room believing that he had, unaided, in a salt town, arrived at something.
He had. That is the worst part. He had.

Then he put the pot down and said:
"You must be tired, Sayyid. Carrying it."
I said something about the season.

I would like to report that I did something. There was nothing to do. There is no move from that position; I have looked for one for twenty years and there is no move. I sat under the window of a good house with a fig tree in it and my ears made a noise.
He said, "Not the town. God forbid. The town would be extremely upset." He laughed, the door-in-a-draught. "Four of us. Myself, and three others, and one of them is dead now."
"The first Friday."

"By Qom."

"By whoever is doing it that year." He shrugged with his eyebrows. "And they send us — Sayyid, forgive me, but they send us either a young man who is here as a punishment and wants to be gone by spring, or they send us a serious one."

"A serious one," said Haj Rasoul Sarmadi, "writes reports."
The fig tree moved in the window.

"And I don't have a teacher in Qom."

I have been threatened by professionals. I want to say clearly that nothing has ever been done to me as thoroughly as that sentence, delivered by a seventy-one-year-old man refilling a glass I was not drinking from, with real affection, as a compliment.
"So it isn't that I'm useful," I said. "It's that I'm not able."

"It's both. That's why it's good." He sat back. "You're better than the last four. "And if I'd been a fraud who was no good?"
"Then you'd have been a fraud who was no good," he said, "and we'd have managed, and in three years there'd have been a transfer."
We looked at each other for a while.
"Haj Rasoul."
"Sayyid."
"What happened to Sayyid Hadi Vahedi?"
And the old man's face did not change at all, which is the answer, and he said:

I have gone over the rest of that afternoon many times and there is nothing in it. We talked about the tiles. He walked me to the gate with his hand under my elbow, which he always did, and he said the thing he always said, which was you'll say if there's anything, and I said I would say.
Here is what I understood on the walk back along the wall.

For eleven months I had been congratulating myself on a magnificent piece of work. I had thought I was a man who had got in. I had thought — God, the vanity of it, I can hardly write it down — I had thought that I was running a long, elegant confidence operation on nine hundred people.
I had been running nothing. I had been acquired.

The tin on the first night was not a temptation, it was an aptitude test. The freedom to do as I liked in that town was not the negligence of a trusting old man, it was policy. Every single thing I had taken as evidence of my own skill was a fitting. And I had spent eleven months wagging.
A rope you can work at. A rope is a relationship; a rope has two ends and one of them is yours.
I had been on a leash since the first Friday and I had been trotting.

Everyone in the building has made my arrangement. That is not a comfort.
I did not sleep that night and what kept me up was not Haj Rasoul.

It was the man in the corridor in Kashmar with the knee, who had not believed in any of it for twenty years, and who stayed because somebody had to bury eleven hundred mothers properly and he was not prepared to hand the job to a boy from Qom.
Because on Sunday afternoon I had finally understood what he was.

He was on a leash too. Of course he was. He had a district and a stipend tier and a bishop somewhere who knew exactly what he was worth and exactly how little he could do about it, and there were men above him doing something with a cement plant, and he knew, and he stayed, and every funeral he conducted was simultaneously the most decent act available to a human being in that province and a small piece of maintenance work on the machine that was running the cement.

And there is no way out of that. That is the thing I want the boy to understand when he reads this, if he ever does, and I suspect he will read it at exactly the age when it will do him the most harm.

There is no version where you do the good thing and not the other thing. The coat that lets you into the worst hour of a stranger's life is the same coat, the identical object, the actual physical garment, that the men with the cement are wearing. You cannot go into that room in your own clothes. Nobody will let you in. And once you are in it, you are in it, and the good you do in there is real — I insist on this, I have seen it, I have done it, fourteen people slept better because of a question about a saucepan — and it is also, at the same time, a small deposit into an account that is not yours and that you will never see the balance of.

I have been a criminal all my life and I have never had to hold two things like that at once. In my trade the arithmetic is simple: you take a thing, they lose the thing. It is honest work in the sense that no part of it requires you to believe anything.
I lay on a transparent carpet in Shurabad and turned it over until first light and I could not get it to come out.
And then, at about five in the morning, with the salt going in the walls, I had the thought that I would call the worst thought of my life if I did not know that it was simply true, and it was this:
I am the only one in the building who is here for nothing.

Because they had all made the arrangement for a reason. The knee had eleven hundred families. The corpse-washer had thirty-one years and a wife two years gone. Haj Rasoul had a town, a kitchen, a grandson's job. Mojtaba had fourteen pages and a rope thrown to a man who could not swim.
And I had put the coat on because it was on a chair and nobody was watching it.

That is what I could not get past, at five in the morning, and it is the only thing in this entire account that I would still call shame, in the technical sense, and I have thought about it every week for twenty years.
Everybody else in that building had paid to get in.

She has her mother's flatness and my jokes, and I did the only paternal act available to a man in my position, which was surveillance.
In the third week of the forty days I ran a check on the man my daughter was marrying.
I want to describe how, because it is the most sordid thing I did in Shurabad and it is also, technically, the first act of fatherhood I had performed since 2010.

The clergy of this country are not a hierarchy. They are a network, which is a different animal, and I had eleven months of standing next to it. Every man in that Kashmar hall had a district. Every district has a mosque, and every mosque has a man who knows who everybody's family is, and the whole thing runs on telephone calls that begin with four minutes of health enquiries and end with somebody saying ah, that family, yes.
I knew the town from the folder. She had left the folder on the desk for four days.

So I made a telephone call to a man I had met once in a corridor, and I asked after his knee, and his mother, and the tiles, and then I said that a family from his district had approached the shrine on a matter and I wished to know, in confidence, whether they were people of good standing.
And he told me. Four minutes. Everything.

There is no privacy in this country. There is an enormous amount of modesty and no privacy whatsoever, and the two things are not related, and I had spent my whole criminal career admiring this fact from the outside without once being on the inside of it.

The man's name was Farid [fa-REED]. He was twenty-six. He worked in the parts department of an agricultural machinery dealership, he had two sisters, his father had died of the heart in 2019, he was regarded as reliable, he had never been in any trouble at all, and there was a slight embarrassment in the family about an uncle and a loan.
He was fine.
That is what I got, in the office, at eleven o'clock at night, with a telephone in my hand and my heart going: he is completely fine.
I sat with that for a long time.

Because I had been prepared. I had written the whole film. I had cast myself extremely well in it.
And the boy sells tractor parts and has never been in any trouble at all.

There was nothing for me to do. There has never been anything for me to do. I said thank you, and asked again about the knee, and put the telephone down.
And what I did next is the part I would remove if I were making myself look good.

I put my future son-in-law in my notes like a job.

The uncle is a real thing and the loan is a real thing and there was, four years later, an occasion when it mattered, and I did something about it from a distance, and neither of them will ever know, and I am not going to describe it here because it is the only clean thing I own and I would like to keep one.

That is true. That is literally, physically, forensically true, and it was true in the courtroom and it is true now, and I have said it to myself perhaps ten thousand times since, and here is what I have to report about it:

Then I heard the ambulance on the street and I went out of the window.
They had me in nine days.

She had a fracture at the top of the femur and they pinned it and she was walking with a frame by the spring. She died in October, of pneumonia, which is what happens, which is what the doctor said happens, which is what my own lawyer said in mitigation with a great deal of energy, and the judge in Mashhad listened to it all and did not appear to find it as decisive as we did.

The woman in the corner-by-the-window house in Shurabad, in the third month, the first funeral I ever conducted, the one who died in her sleep and about whom fourteen people argued for ninety minutes about which of them she had preferred, was eighty-four years old.

I sat in the corner of that room and drank four glasses of tea and did my mother's trick and could not find the seam and went home disturbed and put the whole thing in a drawer, and it took me another nine months to open the drawer, and when I opened it there was nothing in it except a very small woman in a corridor holding a glass of water that did not break.

I do not know what else to do with the sentence. A room built for a purpose will tell you the purpose. It has nothing else to talk about.

A burglar looks at a room and sees what it is for now, and underneath that what it was for before, and underneath that what somebody changed and when and how much it cost them, and a room cannot lie about this, because a room is made of the decisions people paid money for.
Four paces by five. Stone. Barrel vault, low. Door on the east, single, heavy, no second exit. Grave in the centre under the lattice.
And the vent, high on the north wall, bricked.
Here is what I found in an hour with a tape measure and no candle.

You do not pay a mason to close a hole flush and point it to match unless the hole closing matters to you; if you simply want a draught stopped you stuff it, and the shrine of Emamzadeh Nur, God knows, has stuffed plenty.
Two. It is the only aperture in that room other than the door. Four paces by five, stone, and one hole, and somebody closed it.

Three. The door has a felt strip along the bottom edge. Old felt, replaced many times, the current one perhaps five years old and the nails going back through four generations of previous ones. Somebody has been maintaining a seal on the bottom of that door since before my father was born.

Four, and this is the one that made me sit down on the step outside: there are four iron rings set into the floor, one in each quarter, about a hand's width across, set into the stone itself and not into any later screed. Old. Older, I would say, than the dome. They are the feet of the braziers. They stop them travelling.

A brazier does not need a ring in the floor to stop it travelling. A brazier needs a ring in the floor if it is going to be there for eight hours with two men working around it in the dark and nobody able to see where anything is.
Somebody built that room to hold four fires and no air.

I went back to the office and I got the ledgers out and I looked for the mason, and the mason is in there, in 1961, in the hand of Haj Rasoul's father: a payment, and it is not a small payment, and beside it, in the column where the trustees have written a note against every disbursement since 1938, there is a note, and the note says: for the north wall, as before.
As before.

I went back further. I found the previous one in 1919, in a different hand, in the accounts of a different Sarmadi, and the note against that one is the north wall, closed again, which means it had been open, which means somebody had opened it, which means that at some point between those two dates a man had come into that room, looked at the north wall, and decided the room needed air — and had been overruled, at cost, by the family.
Nineteen custodians in eighty-seven years. Nobody stays.
And the last thing I looked for, and I looked for it because I am what I am and because you always check the consumables, was the esfand.

It is in there. Of course it is in there, it is in there every year, it is a legitimate expense, nobody has ever hidden it in the slightest. Sacks. Every year, in the season, in the accounts, openly, between the paraffin and the whitewash, going back to the first page in 1938 and, I have no doubt, back through every book before that one which was lost in the fire.
And I looked at the quantity and I thought: that is a great deal of esfand.
And that is all I thought.

I want to be very precise about my own stupidity here, because it is the largest single failure of my life and it is not a moral failure, it is a professional one, and those are the ones that keep you up.

I had, at that moment, in a room, on a desk, in my own hands: a stone box built to hold fire and no air; a seal maintained on the door for four generations; a vent that had been closed and closed again at expense against the wishes of at least one man who wanted it open; four iron rings in the floor; a reputation across four provinces for people seeing things; and an invoice for sacks of the seed my mother burned over my head when I was nine.
And what I concluded was: they are managing the atmosphere.

That is what I wrote down. I wrote down that the family had, over generations, discovered that a dark sealed room full of smoke and grief produces a powerful experience in a crowd, and had engineered the room to produce it reliably, and had kept it quiet because you cannot advertise it without ruining it.
Which is true. Every word of that is true and I was rather pleased with it.
I did not think about the seed.

Nobody thinks about the seed. That is the whole of it, that is the entire ninety-year business plan, and it is not even a plan, nobody sat down and invented it — you cannot hide a thing better than by putting it in the one category that every single person in the country has agreed not to look at. It is what your grandmother does when you get a promotion. It is what the taxi driver does to his own dashboard. It is not a substance. It is not anything. It is esfand.
I had it in my hand in a room at two in the morning and I put it back in the cupboard, third from the left, spine out.

Go in looking for the trick. Find the trick. Watch it work anyway.
The mourning nights came round again and I went into the chamber on the second night with my eyes open.
I sat at the north wall, under the brick, because Haj Rasoul had told me a year earlier that it was easier there, and because I now wanted very much to know what he had meant.
And I caught all of it.

I saw the two men in rotation. I saw the boy who brings the sacks in from the store on the west side and hands them through the door and does not come in. I saw one of the men, at about the fourth hour, do a thing with the second brazier which I would describe as feeding it up — a double handful, worked into the coals with an iron, in a room that already had sixty people breathing in it and had not had a change of air since ten o'clock.
I saw it. I noted the times. I am, I would like to say, an extremely good witness.
And at the fifth hour the stone breathed and I went with it.

I want to be honest about how little the knowing was worth. There is a thing men in my trade say about drink, that you cannot see through a bottle from inside it, and I had assumed my whole life that this was self-pity. It is not self-pity, it is a technical description. I sat under that brick with a complete and accurate inventory of the mechanism in my head — sacks, rings, felt, vent, 1961, for the north wall, as before — and the mechanism took me apart exactly as thoroughly as it had taken me apart the year before, and the only difference the knowledge made was that this time I was also embarrassed.
Time came apart again. The geometry came.
And my mother was in the room.

Not a vision. I have to keep saying this and I know it does not help. There was no figure and there was no light and nothing appeared. What happened was that Parvaneh was in the room, in the way that a person is in a room when you have your back to them, and I knew where she was, which was slightly behind me and to the left, and I did not turn round because you do not turn round.

She was doing the thing with her hands. Over my head. Three times round, muttering. The thing she did in the kitchen when someone had looked at me too admiringly at a wedding, which I had stood through at nine years old with my eyes shut being embarrassed, and which she had done over me at every threshold of my life — school, the day of my wedding, the day they took me, I am told the day I was born.
And I sat in a stone room in Shurabad at forty-six years of age with my eyes shut, being embarrassed.
And I said, out loud, "I'm sorry about the flat."
Which is not a thing I have ever said to anybody.

Then the queue came back. It came back exactly as it had the year before, which frightened me more than anything else that happened in that room, because I know what I am like and I know that a man who has been given a vision will build it up between one year and the next — will add to it, improve the rhythm of the third clause, the way the man in Bardaskan improved mine. I had been braced for it to be bigger.
It was identical.

Women along a wall, in daylight, in clothes from before I was born. A courtyard I did not know. And near the front, one of them, young, large and loud, carrying something in both arms in the way you carry something you have brought a long way, and her face was the face I had watched go from the sink to the stove for the first thirty years of my life.
She was waiting for something.

She was in a queue, and she was waiting, and behind her the wall was the wall of the courtyard of Emamzadeh Nur, which I had walked along twice a day for a year, and which I did not recognise in that room and did recognise afterwards, at four in the morning, sitting on the step with the cold coming in, when it was too late to look at it properly.
Here is what I decided.
I decided it was grief.

I was a man whose mother had died while he was in prison, who had not been at the funeral, who had not been permitted to be at the funeral, and who had spent four years and eleven months not thinking about it with tremendous discipline. And I had now sat twice in a dark room full of smoke with sixty people who were all thinking about their dead, and my dead had come, as anybody's would.

That is a good explanation. It is a very good explanation. It accounts for everything except the wall of the courtyard, and I decided the wall was suggestion, because I had walked past it twice a day for a year.

I went out at first light and Haj Rasoul was in the courtyard with a glass of tea and said, "It's something, isn't it," exactly as he had the year before, word for word, standing in the same place, looking extremely well rested.
And I said, "Haj Rasoul, when did your father brick the north wall?"
And he said, without any pause at all, "Before my time, Sayyid. Drink that, you're pale."

"And when Zahra [zah-RAA] asked you if she was any relation, you said no, and it was the best thing I have ever seen anybody do. It was beautiful. And I wrote sixty-one down again because my hand had to be doing something."
The salt in the walls.

And Shokouh Aramesh laughed.

She laughed the way you laugh at a funeral when someone does an impression of the deceased complaining about a saucepan — helplessly, horribly, with her hand back over her mouth and her eyes going — and then she stopped, and stood by the door, and neither of us said anything for a while.
Then she said, "Are you going to tell her?"
"No."
"Why not?"
And I said the true thing, because there was no longer any point in the other kind:

"Because she's got a ruling. I gave her a ruling. She asked me if she was permitted to hate him and I sat her down on the wall by the tap and I told her yes, and I made it beautiful, and she wrote it down on her telephone with her thumbs. And it's the only useful thing anyone has ever given her about me." I heard my own voice do something I did not authorise. "If I tell her, she loses the ruling. She'd have to start again, at nineteen, from a man in a coat. She's got a wedding in Ordibehesht."
Shokouh looked at me for a long time.
"You know what you've done, don't you," she said.
"Yes."
"You've made yourself into her priest so you'd never have to be her father."
I did not answer that, and I have not answered it since, and I am not able to answer it now.
She opened the door. Then she stopped, with her hand on it, and said — and this is the sentence that I have kept, out of everything, out of all of it, this is the one I would take with me:
"I'm not going to tell her either."
And she went out and across the courtyard to the kitchen, and that is the moment I stopped being able to leave Shurabad, and everything after this is just the arithmetic of it.

Eleven weeks. Count them.
I have never been with a woman for longer than eleven weeks.

I do not mean married; I was married for seven years. I mean the other thing, the thing I was actually good at, the only professional competence I have ever had that did not involve a window. And the method was not charm — I have no charm, I have a flat voice and a face like a bus timetable — the method was attention.

I listened like it was a trade. I remembered the names of people's sisters. I arrived on time. I noticed when something had changed about a room. For a period of somewhere between six and eleven weeks I was, in each individual case, an extraordinarily good man — better than the men who loved them, materially better, more present, more accurate — and then, at some point in the eleventh week, without any decision being made and without any incident, I would find that I had stopped.
Not left. Stopped. The attention would simply go off, the way a lamp goes off, and what was left behind was a man who could not remember why he had asked about the sister.
I used to think this was a defect of feeling. I was quite proud of it in a small dark way, as a thing that made me interesting.
In the fourteenth month in Shurabad, on the road, with a bag in my hand, I worked out what it actually was, and it is not interesting at all.

Eleven weeks is how long you can pay attention to somebody before you have to know them. That is all it is. It is not a romantic interval. It is the point at which the account of a person you have assembled by watching runs out, and the only way to continue is to be told things, which requires being in the room as yourself, and I have never been in a room as myself in my life.
I had been in Shurabad thirteen months.

That is the number I want in the record, because it is the whole book: I did to nine hundred people what I used to do to women, and it did not stop at eleven weeks, and it did not stop because for the first time the room would not let me leave and would not let me be anybody else either, and the result — the actual measurable result, and I want to be entirely unsentimental about it — is that a town in Khorasan was materially better off, and thirty-two women had a Thursday, and a boy had fourteen pages, and a widow had been told her kitchen was noticed, and a girl had a ruling.
None of which I intended. All of which is real.
I packed in the fourteenth month, on a Tuesday, in the afternoon, with everybody at the tap.

The bag was the dead man's bag. There was almost nothing in it, because I had almost nothing: the comb, the tin of wire hooks, the photograph of the woman who was either his mother or his wife, which I had never been able to throw away. My own telephone. Four hundred thousand tomans that were mine, out of my own stipend, which I had counted twice, because I have never in my life been so careful about the provenance of money as I was that week.
I did not take anything from the tin.
I went out at four in the morning across the courtyard, past the tap, along the wall, and up the one road to the top of the town where the salt starts, and I stood there for a while.

You can see a long way from there. The flat goes white before it goes light. There is a point about six kilometres out where the road stops being a road you can see and becomes a rumour, and the first bus comes through at ten past five, and I had been standing there for forty minutes and it was five o'clock.
And I have been asked what I thought about, and I did not think about my daughter, and I did not think about God, and I did not think about the woman in the corridor.
What I thought about was this: the tea is going to be terrible for the next thirty years and there will be nobody there who says so.
That is it. That is the whole of the moral reasoning of Nader Fani at five o'clock in the morning at the top of a salt town, and I am aware of how it looks, and I have decided not to improve it.
I heard the bus at eight minutes past.

I stood and I watched it come up out of the rumour end of the road, all the way, four or five minutes, headlights and then a shape and then a bus, and it slowed at the top of the town the way they do, and the door opened, and the driver looked out at a sayyid standing at the roadside at ten past five in the morning with a bag in his hand.
And he said, "Aqa? Are you coming?"
And I said, "No. God bless you. I was seeing someone off."

And he shut the door and went, and I walked back down the hill in the wrong shoes and put the comb and the hooks and the photograph back on the shelf, and I was in the courtyard at half past six when Shokouh came out with the bucket, and she looked at the bag by my door, and looked at me, and said:
"There's tea."
"Is it terrible?"
"It's terrible," she said.
And she went and knelt down and started insulting the floor.

When they come to test you, say nothing and let the boy talk.
They sent a man out from Mashhad in the fourteenth month.
He was about fifty, in good cloth, with the accent, and he came in a car with a driver and he was courteous to everybody in a way that took approximately nine seconds to identify as an audit.

Haj Rasoul was delighted to see him. Haj Rasoul was so delighted to see him that I understood within a minute that the old man had not known he was coming and was extremely unhappy about it, and I want to record that this was the first and only time in fourteen months that I saw Haj Rasoul Sarmadi's hands do something he had not authorised.

The visitor stayed two days. He looked at the tiles. He looked at the guest rooms. He asked about the mourning nights, and the numbers, and how we managed the crowds in a chamber that size, and Haj Rasoul talked about ventilation for eleven minutes without once using the word.
And on the second evening, in the office, with tea, he turned to me.
It was not aggressive. It was worse than aggressive; it was collegial. He asked me where I had studied. He asked it the way you ask a man where he grew up.

Now, I had a story. Obviously I had a story — I had had a story since the fourth day, I had polished it for fourteen months, and it was a good story, and it would not have survived four questions from a man in good cloth with the accent.
I did not use it.

I did the thing. I looked at the middle distance with an expression of mild sorrow and I let eleven seconds go past, and then I said, "It was a long time ago and I don't think about it much," which is a sentence with a hole in the middle of it, and I watched him decide whether to put his hand in the hole.
He decided to. He was good.
He said, "Under whom, though? I only ask because there's a — forgive me — there's a quality to the way you handle a room, and one hears it and one wonders whose it is."
And Mojtaba Sadeghpour, nineteen years old, sitting at the side with the tea things, said:
"Forgive me, Aqa."
Everybody looked at him.
And that boy — that boy, in a room with a man from Mashhad who could have ended his career with a telephone call, on his own initiative, having been asked nothing —
He gave him page eleven.

He gave him the rope and the water. He gave him the whole argument, from the top, carefully, with the it may be that I am mistaken, and he built it in front of a hostile professional in about four minutes: that a chain is a device for carrying a thing and not the thing; that the question of whose it is, is downstream of the question of whether it lands; that a man may stand where the tradition stood before anybody had needed to write anything down.
And then he did something I had not taught him and could not have taught him, because it requires a kind of nerve I do not possess.
He turned it into a compliment.

He said that he had noticed the same quality in the Aqa's own manner over the last two days, and that he had wondered whose it was, and that he had concluded — with respect — that it was probably nobody's, and that this was the highest thing one could say about a man in this line.
There was a silence.
And the man from Mashhad laughed, and put his glass down, and said, "Where did you find him?"
And I said, "He was sent."
They talked about Qom for the rest of the evening and the audit was over, and the car left at nine the next morning, and Haj Rasoul walked it to the gate with his hand under the driver's elbow.

I want to describe what I felt watching a nineteen-year-old defend me with an argument I could not have made, in a language I cannot read, against a man who had come to find exactly what he had found and went home without it.
It was not gratitude and it was not pride.
It was the specific sensation of watching a man sign a document without reading it, when you are the one who put it in front of him.

The generous offer is the cage. They are always generous. That is how the door shuts quietly.

The letter came in the fifteenth month, in a brown envelope with a provincial stamp, addressed to the Custodian, Emamzadeh Nur, and Mojtaba brought it in with the rest and I opened it with a knife while he was talking about something else.
It was a circular. It went to every shrine and every mosque of any size in the province, which is perhaps four hundred of them, and it was about a programme.

There is an office now that arranges for clerics to go into the prisons and sit with the men. Not to preach — the letter was quite emphatic about this, and the emphasis was the tell, because a man who is not preaching does not need to say so twice. To sit with them. To be present in their process of return.

It was a good letter. That is what I want to convey. It was written by somebody who believed every word of it, and it made an argument I have never been able to knock down, which is that a man in a cell is in the worst hour of his life and that somebody ought to be allowed in there who is not employed by the institution that put him in it.
It invited the custodian to indicate his willingness.
And at the bottom of the second page, above the stamp, there was a name and a rank.
I sat in that office for a long time with my thumb on it.

He had gone up. Of course he had gone up; men like that always go up, because the statistics are real and because he genuinely did not steal anything. He had a province now. He had four hundred shrines and a programme and a form for indicating willingness, and he had spent his entire working life on a single sincere idea, which is that men are made good by pressure, and here at last was pressure with a warm face on it.

And I understood that if I indicated my willingness, I would be driven in a car to the gate of a prison in this province, and I would go in wearing this coat, and men who had known me as Panjshanbeh would be brought into a room to be sat with.

I also understood, holding the letter, that this was not a trap. That is the part that has never stopped being funny to me in the specific way that things are funny at four in the morning. There was no trap. There was no cleverness. Sarhang Zaker had no idea where I was, had probably not thought about me in three years, and the letter had gone to four hundred addresses. The cage was not built for me. The cage is simply the shape of the world and I had walked into a corner of it by accident, which is the only way anybody ever does.
Mojtaba said, "Will you go, Sayyid? They say it counts for a great deal."
"It does count," I said. "It counts for a great deal."
And I took a pen and I wrote across the bottom of the reply slip, and what I wrote was:
I cannot come. May God keep you well.
Eight words. I counted them at the time and I have counted them since, and it remains the only piece of correspondence in my life that I would not change.

I gave it to Mojtaba to post and he posted it, and four hundred shrines indicated their willingness or did not, and a man in a provincial office read a slip from a salt town at the end of a road and put it on a pile, and that was the end of it, and I have never in twenty years stopped waiting for it not to be the end of it.

There is no witnessing. I invented it in eleven minutes at half past four in the afternoon to buy six weeks. But she had come four hundred kilometres for it, and Mojtaba had asked me twice what the form of it was, and so on the morning of the twenty-first I performed it.

We did it in the courtyard, by the tap. Mojtaba stood at my right with the register. Shokouh stood at the door of the kitchen with her hands in front of her and did not come closer. I said what I had made up. Some of it was in Arabic. It was four clauses, and it was about the going-out of a man from a house, and the house continuing, and it was among the better things I made in that town.
Then I sat down at the table with the pen.

The statement was three paragraphs, in my hand, on shrine paper with the stamp. I wrote her father's name in my own hand.
I wrote it slowly, because the pen was bad, and because I had not written it in four years, and I looked at it on the paper for a moment before I went on.
Then I signed it, and I stamped it, and I dated it, and I gave it to her.
She read it standing up. She read it twice. And then she said, "That's it, then," in the flat voice, her mother's voice, and she folded it once and put it in the plastic wallet with everything else.
"Thank you, Haj Aqa."
"It's nothing."
"It's half a year of my life," she said. "It's not nothing."
She put the wallet under her arm. Then she said, "Can I ask — is it wrong that I'm not sad?"
And I said, "No."
"Everyone keeps waiting for me to be sad."
"Then they'll wait."

She nodded. She looked around the courtyard, at the tap and the wall and the blue dome, in the way that people do when they are fixing a place in order to be able to say afterwards that they went there.
"It's a good place," she said. "It's very quiet."
"It's the salt."
"Right." She put out her hand to shake mine and then remembered, and took it back, and laughed at herself, and said, "Sorry. Sorry."
"It's all right."
"Goodbye, Haj Aqa."
"Goodbye."

She went across the courtyard and out through the gate, and Shokouh was still standing at the door of the kitchen with her hands in front of her, and she did not move for a long time after the gate had shut.

Take the student. Do it knowing exactly what you are.
The bus goes at ten past nine and I did not walk her to it.

I stood at the office window instead, at an angle, the way you stand at a window when you do not wish to be seen standing at a window, and I watched my daughter walk up the one road in Shurabad with a plastic wallet under her arm, and get onto a bus, and I watched the bus go down the hill and become a shape and then headlights and then a rumour.

I have been asked whether I nearly went after her. I did not nearly go after her. There was no nearly. A man who has spent his life in stairwells does not have a nearly; he has a sequence of small decisions that were each individually correct, and at the end of them a bus.
At about eleven o'clock Mojtaba came and found me and said that he had written to Qom.
I said, "About what?"
"To extend," he said. "The six months finished in Dey [DEY] and nobody wrote and I didn't say anything, and I've written now to ask for two years."
"Two years."
"Or three." He was standing extremely straight. "Sayyid — I would like to ask formally. To read with you. Properly. As a student."
The stove ticked.
Here is the accounting, done at the time, in the four seconds available, and I want it entered exactly as it was, without improvement.

I knew that the boy could not read with me because there was nothing to read with. I knew that his mother thought he was in Mashhad. I knew that he had built fourteen pages of scaffolding to hold up a decision he had made about a man who did not exist, and that he had now defended it in front of a professional and won, and that the winning had welded it. I knew that if he stayed two years he would be, at twenty-one, a man with a brilliant argument and no ground under it, and that the ground would go at some point in his thirties, in a room, in front of somebody, in some way I could not predict and would not be there for.
And I knew that I had watched him sign the document I put in front of him and I had not read it out to him.
Four seconds.
I said, "Three years."
He went red to the ears and thanked me and went out to write to Qom again to correct the number, and I sat in that office and listened to him going up the passage two steps at a time.

That is the whole of it. That is the man. I have written five parts and thirty-nine of these and if you want the entire thing in one movement it is a man at a window watching a bus become a rumour, turning round, and taking a student.
I started writing these that night.

I am not going to say here who they are for, because he does not know yet, and because there are things I have to set down before I can put his name in the same sentence as my own. He will work it out. He will be angry for about a year and then he will not be, and that is a thing I have no control over and have made my peace with, which is a lie, and I have left it in.

Burn it yourself.
Three nights later I went into the chamber alone and lit the braziers.

It was not the season. There was nobody in the town who needed anything. The reason I did it is not available to me even now and I have stopped hunting for it; I have come to think that a man who has spent his whole life being unable to say why he did things should be allowed one occasion where that is simply the truth.
I took the key off the hook. I opened the door and let it stand open for a while.

The iron rings in the floor, one in each quarter. The felt along the bottom edge. The brick in the north wall, flush, pointed to match, paid for in 1961 and before that in 1919, for the north wall, as before.
I set two of the four braziers, not all four, because I am not a fool, and I lit them, and I took the sack from the west store and I did what my mother did.
A double handful. Onto the coals.

And it went off the way it goes off — the small hard crackle, the noise every single person born in this country knows before they know their own name — and the smoke came up, and I stood in a stone room under a blue dome in a salt town four hundred kilometres from the flat where I was born, and I smelt my mother's kitchen.
Then I went round three times, over my own head, with my hand, muttering, the way she did.
I have done a great many stupid things and that is the one I would keep.

I sat down under the brick for a while and nothing came. There was no attention in the room. There was smoke and there was stone and there was a man of forty-six in the wrong shoes, and after perhaps an hour I put the braziers out and swept, and left the door open, and went back to the office to do the register.

Because there is a register. There is always a register. Every pilgrim who stays a night at Emamzadeh Nur goes into a book, and has done since 1938, name and town and what they came for, and the books go in the same cupboard as the ledgers, and Haj Rasoul had asked me on the Sunday to find a date for him out of the old ones for something to do with the guest rooms.
He wanted 1979.

I want to be clear that this was not a search. I have looked for things in the dark all my life and I know what looking feels like and this was not it. An old man asked a favour about the guest rooms and I opened a book.

It is a wide page, ruled in four columns: the name, the town, the purpose, and the last one which is narrow and which the trustees have used, on and off for ninety years, for whatever they felt was worth writing.
The hand is Haj Rasoul's father's. I knew it from the mason's payment. He wrote small and he wrote badly and he did not join anything.

And a third of the way down the page for the month of Aban [aa-BAAN], in the year 1357 of our calendar, which is the autumn of 1978, in a town at the end of a road that I had walked out to the top of and come back from, is:
Parvaneh Fani. Tehran.
I did not move.
I have sat in stairwells for four hours and I did not move, and then I put my finger on the paper, which I had never once done to any document in that building, and I went across the page.
The third column, the purpose, says: chelleh.
Forty nights.

My mother came to this town in the autumn of 1978 and stayed forty nights, and I was born the following summer, and she never mentioned it, and she never mentioned it, and she went to her grave without mentioning it, and she burned that seed over my head at every threshold of my life from the day I was born until the day they took me away, and I stood in that chamber four hours ago and burned it over myself.
And in the fourth column, the narrow one, the one they use for whatever they think is worth writing, in the bad small hand that does not join anything, there is a name.
It is the name of the custodian who attended her.
It is the name that is on the identity card in the pocket of the coat I am wearing.
Glossary
Pronunciation is given as plain English syllables; the syllable in
CAPITALS carries the stress. abaya [a-baa-YAA] — Arabic ʿabāʾah, cloak. The loose black outer cloak worn over the qaba by Shi'a clergy; in this book, the garment Shokouh remakes by eye.
Aban [aa-BAAN] — Middle Persian, from the Avestan āpō, "the waters"; the eighth month of the Iranian calendar, late October to late
November. Also, in Zoroastrian usage, the divinity of the waters — a name older than the calendar that carries it.
amameh [ah-maa-MEH] — Arabic ʿimāmah, turban. The wound cloth of the clerical turban. Black denotes claimed descent from the Prophet; white denotes a cleric without that descent.
bismillah [bes-mel-LAAH] — Arabic, "in the name of God." The invocation that opens almost every formal utterance, recitation, meal, and journey.
chelleh [chel-LEH] — Persian, from chehel, forty. A period of forty days or nights undertaken for devotion, retreat, mourning, or petition. Forty is the load-bearing number of Persian life.
esfand [es-FAND] — Persian; the seed of wild rue, Peganum harmala.

Burned on coals to turn away the evil eye, with a characteristic crackle and smoke recognised by every Iranian. Contains the β-carboline alkaloids harmine and harmaline; argued by some scholars to be the haoma of the Zoroastrian sacrifice.
Emamzadeh [eh-maam-zaa-DEH] — Persian, "descendant of an Imam."
Both the descendant and, by extension, the domed shrine built over such a grave. Thousands are scattered across Iran; the occupant of many is disputed.
Haj Aqa [haaj AA-ghaa] — Persian honorific, roughly "reverend sir." The standard address for a cleric whose name one does not know, or does not wish to use.
hadith [ha-DEETH] — Arabic, "report, account." A saying or act attributed to the Prophet, transmitted with a chain of authorities. The chain is called the isnad.
isnad [es-NAAD] — Arabic, "support, backing." The chain of named transmitters attached to a hadith, by which its reliability is assessed.
khanum [khaa-NOOM] — Persian, "lady, madam." Courteous address to a woman, used after the given name.
minbar [MEM-bar] — Arabic, the stepped pulpit in a mosque from which the sermon is delivered.
nazr [NAZR] — Arabic nadhr, vow. A pledge made to God, often at a shrine, and the money, food, or act given in fulfilment of it.
Panjshanbeh [panj-shan-BEH] — Persian, "Thursday," literally "the fifth day." The eve of the Muslim holy day and, in Iran, the night families gather.
qaba [gha-BAA] — Persian/Arabic; the long buttoned coat worn by clergy beneath the abaya.
Qom [GHOM] — City south of Tehran; the principal seat of Shi'a religious learning in Iran.

salavat [sa-la-VAAT] — Arabic, plural of salāt, blessing. The invocation of blessings on the Prophet and his household, called out collectively by a gathering as assent, applause, punctuation, and release.
sanad [sa-NAD] — Persian/Arabic, "document, deed, title." Also, in scholarly usage, a cognate of isnad — the supporting chain.
sayyid [saa-YED] — Arabic, "lord, master." A descendant of the Prophet through his daughter Fatimah. Marked by the black turban. The status can be inherited and cannot be conferred.
sofreh [sof-REH] — Persian, the cloth spread on the floor for a meal; by extension, a votive gathering laid out in fulfilment of a vow.
Shurabad [shoo-raa-BAAD] — Persian, "salt-place," from shur, salty, and the suffix -abad, settled place. A common Iranian toponym; the town in this book is invented.
toman [toh-MAAN] — from the Mongolian tümen, ten thousand. The unit
Iranians actually count in, equal to ten rials; the rial exists chiefly on paper and in the imagination of the state.
Uhud [o-HOD] — The mountain outside Medina, and the battle fought there in 625, in which the Muslims suffered heavy losses.
Vakilabad [va-keel-aa-BAAD] — District of Mashhad, and the name of its principal prison.
